The 20% co-payment option applies to all treatment, not just non-covered care.

How the discount can end early

Old indemnity plans are often riders on a broader policy. Cancelling any other cover on the same policy number, or reducing a sum insured, in the six months before applying means no discount, and doing so during the three discounted years ends it. The look-back period counts only from Nov. 20, so cuts made by Nov. 19 do not count.

There is a way back. A switch can be cancelled without penalty within two business days, freely within three months, and within six months if no claim has arisen. Anyone who withdraws from a switch cannot use the discount again. A later switch without the discount may require underwriting, though the FSC says someone who withdraws within the two-day cooling-off period can switch again without it.

The rider can be dropped only once and cannot be retaken, and its discount can be adjusted by up to 25% a year after the first five years. The switch discount runs to May 22, 2027 for now; the regulators say they will watch for mis-selling and adjust the rules if needed.

Why the regulator wants people out of old plans

The regulator says the old plans' near-full cover made patients less price-sensitive and pushed up the use of non-essential care, and with it premiums.

The 50% discount, it says, was negotiated with insurers on the basis of what the switch is worth to them, and set to be as favourable to consumers as possible. It also notes that the oldest plans have steadier loss ratios than the third- and fourth-generation plans, so broader cover does not always mean higher loss ratios.

The rule on cancelling other cover is aimed at sales staff. The regulator says agents might push clients to switch, cancel their existing policies and put the premium savings into new products. Agents may not pitch the switch unless the customer asks, and buyers get a two-business-day cooling-off period.

A separate measure: finding unclaimed bills

At the same meeting the FSC said the Silson24 claims app will add a tool in the first quarter of 2027 that, with users' consent, matches card payment records against insurers' claims data to find unclaimed bills from the past three years, which it puts at up to 1 trillion won ($750 million). Claims lapse after three years.

As of Nov. 18, 57,258 hospitals, clinics, public health centers and pharmacies, 54.2% of the total, can send bills straight to insurers through the app. Others still require paper forms. The government aims for 80% to 90% by the end of the year.

item.title: Transshipment makes up 60% of Busan's Q3 container traffic, up 20% from a year earlier
item.description:
An airline hub and a direct stop

If you manage freight between third countries and are weighing a routing through South Korea, the first thing to know is that its two big port cities do different jobs. Busan, on the southeast coast and Korea's largest port, works like an airline hub: big ships drop off containers so other ships can carry them on. Incheon, the port city west of Seoul that is also home to Korea's main international airport, works more like a direct stop for nearby Asian routes. Third-quarter figures from Korea's Ministry of Oceans and Fisheries show the split clearly.

The key is transshipment: cargo that is not imported into Korea but moved from an arriving ship to a departing one. In July–September, Korean ports handled 4.19 million TEU of transshipment, up 20.7% from 3.47 million a year earlier. A TEU, or twenty-foot equivalent unit, is the industry's standard measure: one TEU is one 20-foot container. Korea's own import and export containers fell 1.1% to 4.34 million TEU. Of 8.58 million TEU handled in total, almost half was transshipment.

4.09 million TEU changed ships in Busan

Busan handled 6.77 million TEU in the quarter, up 11.2%. Its own import-export volume slipped 0.3% to 2.68 million TEU, while transshipment rose 20.3% from 3.40 million to 4.09 million TEU. That means 60.4% of Busan's throughput was transshipment, and Busan accounted for 97.6% of all transshipment in Korea. By partner region, Busan's transshipment linked to China rose 25.9%, to the US 19.2% and to Europe 108.4%. The ministry did not publish the European base, so only the growth rate is known.

The ministry attributed the jump to ships diverting to Busan and to Gwangyang, a port on the south coast west of Busan, while typhoons congested Chinese ports, and to Busan's growing role as a hub. Gwangyang's transshipment rose 50.2% to about 80,000 TEU. The ministry does not split the increase between the two causes. Busan's total container growth peaked in August at 15.4%, against 8.7% in July and 9.8% in September; the ministry did not link the monthly pattern to specific storms.

Incheon: a door to nearby ports

Incheon is the opposite case. Of its 860,000 TEU in the quarter, transshipment was just 12,000 TEU, or 1.4%. Volume fell 2.1%, which the ministry put down to typhoons in southeastern China delaying ship schedules and causing more vessels to skip Incheon.

Korea Customs Service counts of loaded containers by departure port and destination, for November 2025 to October 2026, make the pattern sharper. The count may include some boxes transshipped in Korea. Of loaded containers leaving Korean ports for the US, 98.7% departed from Busan, from either Busan New Port, the deep-water terminals west of the city where large ocean ships call, or the older North Port near downtown. The share was 98.7% for Germany, 99.8% for the Netherlands and 99.7% for Mexico. Busan also handles more than half of short-sea traffic, but Incheon took 22.7% of loaded containers leaving Korea for Vietnam, 24.4% for Hong Kong and 17.6% for China, and received 29.2% of those arriving from Vietnam.

By value, the airport is the bigger road

Counting boxes and counting dollars tell different stories, and transshipped cargo is not counted in Korea's export value at all. By our calculation from customs data by port, 55.8% of Korea's export value left through airports in the 12 months to October 2026, up from 37.6% a year earlier. In October alone, Incheon International Airport by itself shipped $72.3 billion of Korea's $115.4 billion in exports, or 62.6%. Busan's two port areas together shipped 15.2%.

In the same month, semiconductor exports rose by $40.8 billion from a year earlier, to $56.7 billion from $15.9 billion, while airport exports rose by $47.6 billion, to $72.4 billion from $24.8 billion. The chip figure comes from the customs service's preliminary product data, and the port data do not show what was on each shipment, so we cannot say how much of the airport increase was chips. Exports shipped by sea and other non-airport routes grew 23.9%, from $34.7 billion to $43.0 billion. In short, Busan is big by box count; airports are big by value.

Who earns, and which rules apply

Transshipped cargo is not a Korean import. Korea's Customs Act defines transshipment as moving goods from an arriving vessel or aircraft to a departing one within the same customs district (Article 2), and levies duty on imported goods (Article 14). Transshipped boxes must in principle be reported to customs and checked (Article 141), but they pay no Korean duty. The revenue goes instead to terminal handling and port fees in Busan, and to the carriers that route cargo through it.

The rule shippers most need to know is origin. Under US country-of-origin marking rules (19 CFR 134.1(b)), another country becomes the country of origin only if the goods undergo a 'substantial transformation' there. Changing ships is not a transformation, so goods made in China that pass through Busan are still Chinese-origin goods. Routing through Busan can help cargo avoid congested ports; it does not change the country of origin.

Where Korea fits, and what to watch

Put together, Korea offers three distinct routes: Busan for ocean cargo changing ships, Incheon port for direct short-sea links across Asia, and the airports, mostly Incheon, which now carry more than half of Korea's export value. For third-country cargo that needs to change ships, Busan is where nearly all of it happens, handling 97.6% of the country's transshipment. Fourth-quarter figures will show whether the jump holds once the typhoon effect the ministry cited has passed. Freight-rate trends by route are on our Korea Trade freight page. Korea's next preliminary trade figures, for Nov. 1–20, come out at 9 a.m. Korean time on Monday, Nov. 23 (7 p.m. Sunday in New York).

item.title: The $25 minimum wage bill has two versions. Only the Senate's makes $25 a floor
item.description:
Same name, different $25

The Living Wage For All Act, led by Rep. Delia Ramirez (D-Ill.) and Sen. Chris Murphy (D-Conn.), would raise the federal minimum wage from $7.25 an hour to $25. The House version, H.R. 8555, was introduced on April 28, 2026; the Senate version, S. 4981, followed on July 14. Democrats won both chambers in the Nov. 3 midterms and take control in January, which makes the fine print worth reading now.

The two texts share a name and a dollar schedule, so they are often treated as one bill. Read side by side, they are not. In the House bill, $25 is a target that sits under a ceiling. In the Senate bill, $25 is a floor.

The federal minimum has been $7.25 since July 24, 2009. Adjusted with the Bureau of Labor Statistics consumer price index, that is $11.36 in October 2026 dollars. In other words, $7.25 buys 36% less than it did in 2009.

The House bill caps itself

The House bill defines a large employer as one with 500 or more workers or at least $1 billion in annual revenue. Large employers would go from $12 in 2026 to $25 on Jan. 1, 2031; smaller employers would reach $25 on Jan. 1, 2038. The first step, set for Jan. 1, 2026, was already in the past when the bill was introduced.

The catch is Section 5. If the scheduled rate for a year would exceed two-thirds of that year's national median hourly wage, the minimum is set at two-thirds instead. For years without data yet, the Labor secretary would use Congressional Budget Office projections.

The bill names the Bureau of Labor Statistics but not a specific survey. Using the BLS occupational wage survey, the national median hourly wage for May 2025 was $24.51, and two-thirds of that is $16.34. For the full $25 to apply, the median would have to reach $37.50, 53% above where it is now. Until then, the minimum would be the lower of the scheduled rate and two-thirds of that year's median.

In the Senate bill, $25 is the floor

The Senate bill counts years from its effective date, the Jan. 1 after enactment, rather than from fixed calendar dates. It has no cap. From the year after it reaches $25, the minimum each year becomes the greater of the prior year's rate or two-thirds of the median wage, as measured by the BLS Current Population Survey, so it can rise but never fall.

If the bill became law in 2027, it would take effect on Jan. 1, 2028. Large employers would reach $25 in 2033 and others in 2040. The 2031 and 2038 dates often cited come from the House text.

Tips stop counting toward pay

Federal law now lets employers pay tipped workers $2.13 an hour in cash and count up to $5.12 in tips toward the $7.25 minimum, topping up only when tips fall short. That allowance is known as the tip credit.

Both bills phase it out. Large employers' cash wage would rise from $6 in year one to $9, $12, $15 and then $18 in year five, and match the regular minimum five years after the law takes effect. Other employers would start at $4.75 and add $1.75 a year. The bills also write into law a worker's right to keep tips.

For a server on a 40-hour week in a state that follows the federal floor, the employer's minimum cash pay would rise from $85.20 a week today to $240 in year one at a large employer. Opponents argue that a jump in labor costs could push small businesses to cut jobs and hours. Whether that cost shows up in menu prices, fewer hours or smaller tips is where restaurant owners and wage advocates part ways.

Seven states, including Alaska, California, Nevada, Oregon and Washington, already require the full state minimum before tips. Washington, D.C., went further and then pulled back. Voters approved phasing out the tip credit in 2022. In July 2025 the D.C. Council voted 7-5 to slow the increases and cap the tipped wage at 75% of the regular minimum, reached in 2034.

How far behind the US is

For comparison, South Korea's minimum wage for 2027 is 10,700 won an hour, about $7.99 at the Nov. 18 rate of 1,338.8 won per dollar. The proposed $25 would be about 33,470 won.

The OECD compares minimum wages with the median wage of full-time workers. On that measure the US stood at 24.1% in 2025, the lowest of the 32 countries in the data. South Korea was at 59.6%, Britain 61.9% and France 62.5%. Only Colombia, Costa Rica and Mexico topped two-thirds. The bills use the median of all workers, part-timers included, which is lower. Against that yardstick, $7.25 is about 30%.

What's next

The current Congress ends on Jan. 3, 2027, and bills that have not passed die with it. Sponsors would have to reintroduce it in the new Congress. The first thing to watch is whether the House version drops its cap to match the Senate text, and what start date it uses.

The votes are still hard to find. Ending a filibuster takes 60 votes in the Senate. President Trump could veto the bill, and overriding him takes two-thirds of both chambers. For employers, including Korean restaurant and retail chains in the US, local rates already set the bar: $18.40 in Washington, D.C., and $17.13 in Washington state.

item.title: Korean ramen exports jump 24%, with Mexico and UK growing fastest; seaweed prices to Japan slide 23%
item.description:
Where Korean ramyeon is going

If you import Korean instant noodles, two questions matter most: are other markets buying more, and can Korean factories take bigger orders? South Korea exported $1.98 billion of ramyeon, or Korean instant ramen, and similar prepared noodles (HS 190230) in the 12 months to October 2026, up 24.4% from the previous 12 months, according to our calculations from Korea Customs Service data. Volume rose 20.3%.

China ($465 million, up 22.3%) and the US ($372 million, up 26.4%) are still the biggest buyers, taking 42% between them. Growth was fastest in smaller markets. Shipments to Mexico rose from $23 million to $60 million, 2.6 times the earlier figure. The UK was up 48.9%, Canada 43.0% and the Netherlands 30.2%.

Same noodles, different price per kilo

Measured as declared export value divided by weight, the average price rose 3.4%, from $3.92 to $4.06 a kilogram. The gap between markets is wide: US-bound noodles averaged $4.63 a kilogram and UK- and Mexico-bound $4.72, against $3.68 for China and $2.98 for Japan. The code mixes bagged noodles, cup noodles and sauce-heavy stir-fried varieties, so the gaps reflect what each market buys more than what the same product costs.

Monthly exports have kept growing. October 2026 shipments were $183.9 million, up 33.9% from October 2025, when Chuseok, Korea's weeklong harvest holiday (Oct. 3–9), cut working days and flattered the comparison.

Seaweed went the other way

Exports of edible seaweed (HS 121221, which covers dried laver, or gim; seasoned snack laver is classified elsewhere) fell 4.9% to $526 million. Weight fell only 1.4%, so most of the drop came from price. Japan, the biggest buyer, took $127.9 million, down 24.3% from $169.1 million. The weight shipped to Japan dipped just 2.1%, but the average price fell 22.7%, from $14.01 to $10.83 a kilogram.

China moved the opposite way: weight fell 26.8% while the price rose from $16.14 to $20.54 a kilogram. Exports to Russia rose 14.7%. South Korea's Ministry of Oceans and Fisheries said in February that it had expanded laver farming areas for two years in a row. That points to more supply, but the customs data do not show why Japan paid less; Japanese buyers may simply have shifted to cheaper grades. Either way, Korea shipped almost the same weight to Japan and earned $41.1 million less: cheaper for buyers, less revenue per shipment for Korean processors and exporters.

Do Korean factories have room?

For noodles, company filings show how full the plants are. Samyang Foods, the maker of Buldak, said in its third-quarter report that exports made up 1.817 trillion won (about $1.36 billion), or 88.1%, of its 2.062 trillion won in noodle and snack sales in January–September, almost matching its 1.823 trillion won in exports for all of 2025. Its Wonju and Iksan plants ran at 101.4% and 119.0% of standard operating hours, meaning extra shifts beyond the standard schedule. The Miryang plant, which makes mainly export products and accounts for about half of Samyang's noodle capacity, ran at 86.1%. Samyang is spending 207.2 billion won (about $155 million) on eight production lines in Jiaxing, China, with the project scheduled to run until January 2027. Samyang says the plant will serve China's domestic market, but the filing does not say whether shipments from Korea to China will fall once it opens.

Nongshim, the maker of Shin Ramyun, is in a different position. Its consolidated noodle exports were 206.8 billion won (about $155 million) in January–September, and its Korean noodle plants ran at 74.2% of available hours, which Nongshim measures against its maximum available running time rather than Samyang's standard schedule, so the two are not directly comparable. Exports made up only about 9% of Nongshim's consolidated noodle sales, which also include products made and sold by its US and China plants. It is spending 204.3 billion won (about $153 million) on an export-only plant in Noksan, Busan, and in April pushed the end of the investment period to Oct. 30, 2026. According to the Korea Herald and Asia Economy, the plant has recently started running, with capacity of 500 million packs a year, so the 74.2% figure predates it. For buyers, the filings point to different conditions by supplier: Samyang's Wonju and Iksan plants are running beyond standard hours and its export plant in Miryang has nearly 14% headroom, so buyers planning bigger orders may want to confirm early whether Miryang can meet their lead times. Nongshim's new export plant has only just started, so its delivery schedule is worth asking about. Country figures are updated monthly on our Korea Trade ramyeon and laver pages. The next preliminary trade figures from Korea Customs Service, for Nov. 1–20, come out at 9 a.m. Korean time on Monday, Nov. 23 (7 p.m. Sunday in New York).

item.title: More Japanese lenders offer 50-year mortgages, while Korea caps terms at 30 years around Seoul
item.description:
More than half of surveyed lenders now offer 50 years

Home loans that run for up to 50 years have spread fast in Japan. In a survey by the Japan Housing Finance Agency, a government-backed lender, 57.5% of financial institutions set 50 years as the maximum term for variable-rate mortgages, up from 33.8% a year earlier.

For loans with a fixed rate for an initial period, the share rose from 33.6% to 55.2%; for loans fixed for the whole term, from 21.9% to 34.0%. Those figures count lenders offering the product, not borrowers taking it.

The market keeps growing. New home lending to individuals reached 22.9 trillion yen in the fiscal year that ended in March 2026, up 4.2%. Terms have lengthened as house prices climbed, and banks now compete on loan design, including repayment period and loan limits, not only on headline rates, according to the research arm of Shinkin Central Bank, the central institution for Japan's cooperative banks.

What Japan's regulator says it will watch

The Financial Services Agency (FSA) flagged the trend in its annual policy statement, published in September 2026. With interest rates rising, it noted, home loans with repayment periods "markedly longer than before" are being sold.

The statement did not mention 50 years; long terms were its only example. The FSA said it will "carefully monitor," from a consumer-protection standpoint, whether such loans are appropriate given borrowers' expected incomes. It did not ban long terms or set a cap.

The FSA did not spell out its concern, but the trade-offs are plain. A longer term can let a bank lend more to the same customer. The borrower pays less each month but pays interest for longer, and carries the risk of rising rates: 75.0% of Japanese mortgage borrowers chose a variable rate in the agency's January 2026 survey, down from 79.0% in April 2025.

What 50 years does to the numbers

Take a loan of 400 million won (about $299,500) at 1% a year, repaid in equal monthly installments. Over 35 years the payment is 1.13 million won ($846) a month; over 50 years, 850,000 won ($635). That is about 280,000 won ($211) less each month.

But total interest rises from 74.24 million won ($55,600) to 108.46 million won ($81,200). The extra 15 years cost 34.22 million won ($25,600).

Now run the same loan at 2% from the start. The 35-year payment is 17.4% higher, at 1.33 million won ($992). The 50-year payment is 24.5% higher, at 1.06 million won ($790). The longer the term, the larger the share of each payment that is interest, so the payment is more sensitive to rate changes.

Borrowers have moved toward shorter terms

Borrowers' own choices tell a different story from what lenders offer. In the agency's borrower survey, the share with repayment periods over 40 years fell from 7.1% in April 2025 to 5.5% in January 2026.

Those over 35 years fell from 25.5% to 23.4%, while terms of 30 years or less rose from 28.7% to 37.7%. The Shinkin researchers see signs of borrowers choosing shorter terms with rising rates in mind, though terms remain longer than they used to be. They also note that longer terms tend to raise total repayments and the age at which a loan is paid off. The agency does not publish a separate figure for 50-year loans.

Why South Korea went the other way

South Korea's Financial Services Commission (FSC) capped mortgage terms at 30 years in the Seoul metropolitan area and other regulated zones from June 28, 2025. Before that, banks set their own limits, between 30 and 40 years. The FSC said the aim was to close a way around its debt-service ratio rules.

Korea's debt-service ratio, or DSR, limits how much a household can borrow based on the share of annual income that goes to principal and interest on all loans. Stretch the term and the monthly payment falls, so the same income supports a bigger loan.

Take a borrower who can pay 2 million won ($1,498) a month at 4%. Over 30 years they could borrow 418.92 million won ($313,700); over 50 years, 518.53 million won ($388,300). Same income, 99.61 million won ($74,600) more debt.

Questions to ask about any mortgage

The term changes three things at once: the monthly payment, total interest and exposure to rate rises. Asking a lender for the payment and total interest on the same amount over 20 and 30 years makes the trade-off visible. The calculator below runs the same formula.

On a variable-rate loan, the payment after a one-point rate rise shows how much risk the borrower carries. Japan's FSA says it will check whether loans fit borrowers' expected incomes. The Shinkin researchers say it will matter more than before for lenders to explain not just how much can be borrowed but how future rate rises and life plans affect repayment.

item.title: Missed Korea's earned income tax credit in May? You can still claim until Dec. 1, at 95%
item.description:
A Dec. 1 deadline for 260,000 households

South Korea's National Tax Service (NTS) said on Nov. 2 that it was writing to 260,000 households that qualify, or may qualify, for work and child tax credits on their 2025 income but never claimed them. They have until Dec. 1.

The payments are Korea's version of the earned income tax credit: cash for low-income workers, the self-employed and families with children, based on 2025 income. The regular claim window was in May. The law allows late claims for six months after it closes, so this is the last chance for 2025. Payment is scheduled for Jan. 15, 2027. The credit is paid once a year, per household, to one member.

For the first time, the NTS also re-checked income records that employers filed after the March 10 deadline, which had kept some workers off the May mailing list. This year's notices also cover 10,000 households identified that way.

Who qualifies

Eligibility turns on a household's combined 2025 income, including interest, dividends and pensions; its assets as of June 1, 2025, and who was in the household on Dec. 31, 2025. The amount itself is worked out from earnings: wages, business and religious income. For the work credit, total income must be below 22 million won (about $16,500) for a single person, 32 million won ($24,000) for a one-earner household and 44 million won ($33,000) when both spouses work. The child credit covers households with children under 18 and combined income under 70 million won ($52,500).

A one-earner household is one with a spouse who earned less than 3 million won, or a child under 18 or a live-in parent or grandparent aged 70 or older whose own income was no more than 1 million won. It counts as two-earner when each spouse earned at least 3 million won.

Total assets, including the home, car, rental deposit (Korean tenants often hand landlords a large lump sum instead of monthly rent), savings and shares, must be under 240 million won ($180,000). Debt is not subtracted: a home with a government-assessed value of 200 million won, usually below its market price, counts in full even with a 100 million won mortgage.

Households that did not get a notice can still apply through Hometax, the NTS online portal, attaching proof such as an income certificate from their employer; they cannot use the phone line. Households that already took the child tax deduction in their year-end tax settlement get a correspondingly smaller child credit. Young people who did part-time or day work in 2025, and people who have since left their jobs, may qualify.

How the amount is set

The work credit is meant to reward work, so it rises with earnings, stays flat at a maximum, then tapers off. Article 100-5 of the Restriction of Special Taxation Act sets the bands for each household type.

For a one-earner household it rises until earnings reach 7 million won, stays at the maximum of 2.85 million won ($2,140) up to 14 million won, then falls to zero at 32 million won. The maximum is 1.65 million won ($1,240) for single people and 3.3 million won ($2,480) for two-earner households.

The child credit is 500,000 to 1 million won ($375 to $750) per child. One-earner households under 21 million won and two-earner households under 25 million won get the full amount, which then shrinks slowly as earnings rise.

What a late claim costs

Late claims are paid 95% of the full amount. A one-earner household that earned 10 million won in 2025 would have received 2.85 million won in May; claiming now brings 2,707,500 won ($2,030), or 142,500 won ($107) less.

A two-earner household on 30 million won would have received about 1.71 million won, and gets about 1.63 million won ($1,220) now. Actual payments are set by bracket tables in the enforcement decree, so they can differ by a few thousand won.

Assets of 170 million won ($127,600) or more cut the credit in half, on top of the 5% late cut: the one-earner household above would get 1,353,750 won ($1,016). Very small amounts follow fixed rules. Below 15,000 won nothing is paid; on the rising part of the curve anything under 100,000 won is paid as 100,000 won, and on the falling part anything under 30,000 won is paid as 30,000 won. Try your own figures in the calculator below.

What can shrink the payment

The credit is paid as a tax refund: the law treats it as income tax already paid and returns it. So anyone with unpaid national taxes can see up to 30% of the credit applied to that debt first. On a 2 million won credit, that is up to 600,000 won.

If the bank account given on the claim is frozen by creditors, the money may be stuck. Claimants can choose payment in cash instead, collected at a post office with a refund notice sent by registered mail and an ID card.

Misstating income or household details deliberately or through gross negligence bars a claimant from the credit for two years, or five years in cases of fraud.

To guard against scam texts, genuine mobile notices carry a verification mark from the Korea Internet & Security Agency. Households that received a notice can also claim by automated phone line at 1544-9944.

Bigger credits proposed from 2027, not yet law

The government's 2026 tax bill would raise the maximum work credit to 1.8 million won for single people, 3.1 million won for one-earner households and 3.6 million won ($2,700) for two-earner households, and lift the earnings limits to 26 million, 37 million and 52 million won. It would apply to 2027 income and still needs parliamentary approval.

It would also extend the flat, maximum band for two-earner households from 17 million won to 18 million won, to remove a marriage penalty. Today two single people earning 9 million won each get 1.65 million won apiece, 3.3 million won in all; married, their combined 18 million won earns about 3.18 million won. Under the bill the married couple would get the full 3.6 million won, the same as two single people.

For 2025 income, Dec. 1 is the deadline. Eligibility can be checked on Hometax or through the NTS credit helpline at 1566-3636.

item.title: Amazon and United block AI shopping agents as Walmart lets them buy
item.description:
The agent stops at the checkout button

Ask an AI agent to book the cheapest flight to Chicago next week and it will open an airline's site, pick a seat and try to pay. At United Airlines, that last step is now off limits. United added a rule to its contract of carriage on Nov. 11 barring AI agents from buying or changing tickets, and it applies even when a person supervises or approves each step. The airline can cancel bookings made that way. Agents may still show United flights and fares; the customer has to complete the purchase.

United is not alone. eBay's user agreement has barred "any end-to-end flow that attempts to place orders without human review" since Feb. 20. Amazon stopped Meta's Muse agent from shopping its store for customers in September, and its terms, last revised Aug. 14, include a separate section on agents. JPMorgan Chase CEO Jamie Dimon said on the bank's Oct. 13 earnings call that it would not let unvetted outside agents into its systems.

Walmart went the other way on Oct. 21. Each AI agent gets its own profile inside a customer's account. Purchases need approval by default, but the customer can let the agent buy within a cap such as $50, $100 or $200. Shopify has made its Shop Pay checkout available inside outside agents.

What the blockers are protecting

The companies that block agents lead with security. Amazon says agents should "operate openly and respect service provider decisions about whether or not to participate." Amazon has not cited advertising, but a lot rides on it. Its advertising revenue was $19.64 billion in the third quarter of 2026, up 10.9% from $17.70 billion a year earlier. Those ads are sold against search results and product pages that people look at. When an agent searches and chooses for the shopper, fewer people may see those pages.

United cited account and payment security, unintended purchases or mileage redemptions, and federal rules such as the check-in step at which passengers must confirm their bags hold no hazardous items. CEO Scott Kirby put it more bluntly: "I don't want to create another middleman." A company sitting between the airline and its customers could end up owning that relationship and setting the terms of the sale.

JPMorgan has priced access before. In 2025 it said it would charge fintech companies for pulling customer account data, and that September it renewed its data-access agreement with Plaid, which for the first time included pricing. For now, outside AI agents can only read JPMorgan account balances, and only if the customer connects them.

What the openers are after

Walmart promises that "the prices that an AI agent sees are the same prices that a human would see." Its bet is that Walmart goods sell wherever the shopper's agent happens to be. The company says it already works with Meta's Muse, ChatGPT and Gemini, and its dedicated agent gateway starts as a beta for companies and developers.

Shopify has placed itself in the middle of the payment. According to Shop's help pages, for some purchases at stores that do not take Shop Pay, Shop may pay the merchant with a limited-use credential, such as a one-time virtual card, and then charge the customer's card. That puts Shop in the payment flow even at stores that do not run on Shopify.

Who pays when the agent gets it wrong

Liability is the second dividing line. Shop's help pages say purchases a customer approves through an agent are processed as if the customer made them, and a dispute may fail. Walmart says its normal returns process applies even when an agent does not act as intended. Dimon said people using outside agents should understand "the liability transfer."

The courts have weighed in once. On Aug. 4, the U.S. Court of Appeals for the Ninth Circuit vacated the preliminary injunction Amazon had won against Perplexity's agentic browser, holding that under the federal computer fraud law it was the user, not Perplexity, who accessed Amazon's computers, with the agent as a tool. The ruling did not stop companies from restricting access through their terms of service. Amazon's terms, as revised on Aug. 14, require agents to name themselves, not pose as humans and stop when asked.

South Korea offers a preview from a different corner. Figures from Korail, the state-run rail operator, released by a lawmaker's office, show that the ticket-grabbing bot connections it blocked rose from about 460,000 in July to about 36.61 million in September, the month of Chuseok, Korea's autumn harvest holiday, when train travel peaks. The Railroad Business Act only bans habitually reselling or brokering train tickets above their purchase price, with fines of up to 10 million won, or about $7,500. Nothing in it targets software that snaps up tickets first, so authorities have fallen back on charges such as obstruction of business under the Criminal Code. A bill introduced in the National Assembly on Oct. 26 would ban buying tickets by getting around security measures and add penalties. How such a law would treat an AI agent buying for a person could become the next question.

The view from the AI companies

For a company selling an AI agent, a locked door is a business problem: the product shrinks to a search tool that stops before checkout. The route around it is permission. Even Walmart, which opened up, requires agents to use its approved channel and follow its terms, and says it will block those that do not.

As JPMorgan's deal with Plaid shows, an approved route can come with a price. What to watch is who opens a channel first and what they charge for it. Where a company bars agents, it is safer to pay yourself; United, for one, can cancel bookings an agent makes.

item.title: Korea's wrap accounts have no legal single-stock cap, FSS warns, after a client ended up 90% in high-risk KOSDAQ shares
item.description:
90% in KOSDAQ stocks

One Korean investor found 90% or more of a wrap account sitting in high-risk stocks on KOSDAQ, Korea's tech-heavy junior market. The client said the broker had never discussed it and sought damages. The case is one of several the Financial Supervisory Service (FSS), the country's financial watchdog, published on Nov. 16.

A wrap account is a discretionary account: the client hands some or all investment decisions to the brokerage for a fee. It looks like a fund, but the rules are different.

Under Article 81 of Korea's Capital Markets Act, a public fund generally cannot put more than 10% of its assets into securities of a single issuer. Wrap accounts have no legal cap. According to the FSS, many brokers set their own single-stock limits of between 20% and 80%, and some lift them if the client agrees.

That makes two questions worth asking at sign-up: what is the limit on my account, and have I ever agreed to waive it? Clients who find no limit, or one set too high, can ask the broker to set one that fits their risk appetite, the FSS said.

How the account is run matters too. Accounts run one-on-one by a branch adviser, rather than by head office from a model portfolio, can be more volatile, though they aim for higher returns, the FSS said. In one such account, a client complained of losing half the principal after the adviser piled into a few stocks.

Shares you move in can be sold the next day

Another investor moved existing shares into an advisory wrap account, which follows an outside adviser's model portfolio. The next day, all of them were sold without notice.

Shares moved into a wrap account come under the broker's discretion like everything else in it, and can be sold at any time, the FSS said. In its example, one brokerage, as a rule, sells anything not in the adviser's portfolio on the next business day.

Gains and losses belong to the client, the FSS said. Separately, if a holding is suspended from trading, closing the account can be delayed; the FSS said that can happen in normal management and is hard to blame on the broker.

What leaving early costs

At one brokerage the FSS cited, fees come in four parts: an upfront fee on money or shares paid in, a quarterly fee on the average balance, a performance fee on returns above a threshold, and an early-exit fee. None depends on how often the account trades.

If the account is closed within a year, that brokerage keeps 70% of the unused share of the upfront fee. The unused share is the upfront fee times (1 − days invested ÷ 365).

Put in 100 million won (about $74,880) with a 1% upfront fee, or 1 million won ($750). Close after 73 days and the unused share is 800,000 won ($600); the exit fee is 70% of that, 560,000 won ($420). Try your own numbers in the calculator below.

Wrap accounts do not charge separate commissions on Korean stock trades, so staff earn no commission from trading the account frequently, the FSS noted.

A loss on paper, a tax bill anyway

Complaints keep coming from investors in overseas-stock wrap accounts who say nobody explained capital gains tax, the FSS said. Most gains on Korean listed shares are tax-free for small investors, but residents pay tax on gains from foreign shares, and the bill can arrive even when the account is down.

Say a 100 million won account books a 10 million won ($7,490) gain on one stock the broker sold. Another holding is down 15 million won ($11,230) but has not been sold. The account as a whole is 5 million won ($3,740) down.

The tax counts only what was sold. Gains on foreign shares get a 2.5 million won ($1,870) annual allowance per person and are then taxed at 20%, or 22% with local income tax. Here that is 22% of 7.5 million won: 1.65 million won ($1,240).

If the losing stock had been sold in the same year, the loss would have offset the gain. Gains and losses on foreign shares sold in other accounts are pooled too, and the allowance applies once to the total. Losses do not carry over to the next year. Dividends are taxed separately.

What clients can demand

In another complaint, a client said staff ignored a clear request to move to cash and the loss grew. Clients can set reasonable limits on how the account is run, order specific stocks bought or sold, or close the account, the FSS said, and the broker must comply unless it has a legitimate reason not to. Such instructions can get in the way of normal management, such as tracking a model portfolio, so the FSS advises discussing them with staff first.

Clients can also ask to freeze the holdings as they are or to withdraw some cash. In target-conversion wraps, which switch to cash once a return target is hit, a client who asks before the target is reached can have the account closed with the shares still held, rather than sold for cash. Some brokers accept closing or pausing instructions in their apps.

For anyone with an overseas-stock wrap, the next date is May 2027, when this year's capital gains are reported and paid. Asking the broker before year-end how much gain has been realized this year gives a rough idea of the bill.

item.title: Fed Financial Stability Report flags AI data center debt and off-balance-sheet commitments
item.description:
A tenant's lease becomes a developer's collateral

When a large company signs a 15-year lease, the landlord can take that lease to a bank and borrow the money to put up the building. The tenant's credit, in effect, does the borrowing.

That is how many AI data centers are being built. In the Financial Stability Report it released on Nov. 13, the Federal Reserve devoted a box to the arrangement. Hyperscalers, the companies that run the giant clouds (Amazon, Alphabet, Meta, Microsoft and Oracle), sign long-term leases with third-party data center developers. The developers use those leases to raise construction financing.

Leases that have been signed but have not yet started now exceed $1 trillion on an undiscounted basis, the Fed said. The figure is drawn from the filings of seven companies: Amazon, Alphabet, Broadcom, Meta, Microsoft, Nvidia and Oracle.

Chipmakers that guarantee what a GPU will be worth

The second link is the chips. When an AI company borrows to buy graphics processing units, GPU makers often guarantee the residual value of that collateral, promising that the chips will still be worth a set amount years later. With the collateral's value protected, lenders are willing to lend.

On top of that, hyperscalers and GPU designers often take equity stakes in the same smaller firms. The Fed says this creates a "circular financing" dynamic: money a big firm puts into a smaller one can flow back to it as purchases of its chips or cloud capacity.

Guarantees and contract commitments at the seven firms, including take-or-pay contracts that must be paid whether or not the capacity is used, exceed $2 trillion. Add the leases yet to start, and these off-balance-sheet obligations top $3 trillion as of the second quarter of 2026. They have grown even faster than the firms' debt, the Fed said.

Four numbers you can't add together

The report's four headline figures measure different things. The first, more than $680 billion, is debt issued for advanced computing infrastructure through October 2026, about five times the $130 billion issued in all of 2023. Most of it came from investment-grade technology companies. Such borrowing went from less than 6% of nonfinancial investment-grade corporate issuance in 2023 to about 31% this year.

The second, more than $1.1 trillion, is an estimate of public debt still outstanding; private credit deals are too hard to measure and are left out. The third, more than $3 trillion, is the seven firms' off-balance-sheet obligations. The last, close to $1 trillion, is what the largest US bank holding companies have riding on this ecosystem.

The off-balance-sheet figures are not discounted, so they cannot be set directly against debt. A lease paying $100 million a year for 10 years shows up in filings as $1 billion. Discounted at 5% a year, it is worth about $772 million today.

Who takes the loss

The Fed spells out who holds the risk. The debt that hyperscalers and GPU firms carry on their own balance sheets is held mainly by mutual funds, pension funds and insurance companies.

Many of the financings behind these obligations run through special purpose entities (SPEs), which issue both senior and subordinated debt. The riskier subordinated debt and the equity, which absorb losses first, sit with high-yield bond funds, life insurers, business development companies (investment funds that lend to midsize companies) and other private debt vehicles.

The largest US bank holding companies have close to $1 trillion of exposure to big tech firms, data center developers, the special purpose entities, private credit vehicles and utilities. The Fed says those exposures are tested in its annual supervisory stress test.

What worries the Fed, and what could soften the blow

There is a cushion. Because the strongest firms are tied to the weaker ones, they may absorb losses in a downturn and keep them from spreading through the financial system. The flip side is that their real economic exposure may be much larger than their balance sheets show.

The Fed compares the buildout with the broadband telecom investment boom that began in 1995. The five hyperscalers' cumulative capital spending, scaled by GDP, has tracked the telecom industry's closely but has been accelerating and may soon outpace it. Strong cash flow meant the hyperscalers needed less debt than telecom firms did for similar investment, at least until this year.

When the New York Fed polled 23 market contacts in September and October, AI was the most cited risk. In the spring survey it ranked third, behind geopolitical risk and an oil shock. The survey reflects contacts' views, not the Fed's.

Caveats

The Fed says its estimates miss part of the private market, so actual borrowing may be higher. The $3 trillion is an undiscounted total from seven firms' filings, not a forecast of losses. The report does not call the buildout a bubble; it says the interlinkages "necessitate close monitoring."

The same data center can carry very different risk depending on the link: a big firm's own bonds, or the subordinated debt of a special purpose entity, which takes losses first.

item.title: The US overtakes China as the top market for Korean skincare, while UK and Dutch sales surge
item.description:
The US has overtaken China

Korean sunscreens and toners have become fixtures in US drugstores and on Amazon, and export data show how fast that demand has grown. South Korea exported $10.95 billion of skincare products (HS 330499, which covers creams, toners, serums and sunscreens) in the 12 months to October 2026, up 31.0% from the previous 12 months, according to our calculations from Korea Customs Service data.

Shipments to the US rose 39.8%, from $1.47 billion to $2.06 billion. Shipments to China fell 2.5%, from $1.67 billion to $1.63 billion. A year earlier China was ahead by about $200 million; now the US leads by $431 million. China's share of Korea's skincare exports dropped from 19.9% to 14.8%.

Europe: the UK and the Netherlands jump

Growth was faster still in parts of Europe. Exports to the UK rose from $157 million to $439 million, 2.8 times the earlier figure, and to the Netherlands from $83 million to $352 million, 4.3 times. Poland took $344 million, up 60.3%. The Netherlands and Poland are major warehousing hubs, so some of those goods may have been reshipped to other EU countries, but customs data record only the first destination and cannot confirm it.

Prices differ sharply by market. Dividing declared export value by weight, US-bound skincare averaged $27.05 a kilogram, down 3.9% from $28.14, while volume rose 45.4%. The UK average rose from $35.62 to $42.07 and the Netherlands from $40.87 to $49.43. The same code covers large tubs of sun cream and tiny serum ampoules, so the gaps say more about which products each market buys than about what the same product costs.

Supply: factories are expanding, but later than planned

Many Korean beauty brands do not make their own products; they hire original design manufacturers (ODMs), which develop and produce formulas for them. Their latest results point to strong demand, though Cosmax's consolidated figure also includes its plants in China, the US and Indonesia. Cosmax reported third-quarter consolidated sales of 875.8 billion won (about $656 million), up 49.5% from a year earlier. Cosmecca Korea's rose 35.7% to 247.5 billion won (about $185 million).

Their filings on DART, the Financial Supervisory Service's disclosure system, also show when new capacity arrives. In May, Cosmax said it would spend 60.5 billion won (about $45 million) to expand its plant in Pyeongtaek, south of Seoul. On Nov. 2 it amended the filing, pushing the end of the investment period from Oct. 31, 2026 to Jan. 31, 2027. In September, Cosmecca Korea said it would spend 136 billion won (about $102 million) through 2030 on a new plant, which it said would meet rising demand, on top of 64 billion won for the land it agreed to buy in June. New capacity will come in steps, not all at once.

What buyers should check

For US importers, tariffs are part of the landed cost. Since July 24, 2026, US imports of Korean cosmetics have faced total duties of 12.5%, including the Section 301 tariff. The duty is charged on US customs value; using Korea's average declared export value of $27.05 a kilogram as a rough guide, it adds about $3.40 a kilogram. Japanese and Vietnamese cosmetics also pay 12.5%; EU products pay 10%.

Monthly figures show no slowdown yet. Korea's total cosmetics exports (HS 3304) reached $1.155 billion in October 2026, 53.3% more than in October 2025, a month depressed by Korea's long Chuseok holiday. September, when this year's Chuseok holiday fell, was still up 29.4%. With orders still rising and new factory space slipping into 2027, buyers placing orders for next year may want to confirm lead times and minimum order quantities early. Country-by-country figures are updated monthly on our Korea Trade cosmetics page. The next preliminary trade figures, for Nov. 1-20, come out at 9 a.m. Korean time on Monday, Nov. 23 (7 p.m. Sunday in New York).

item.title: Does the Korea-China FTA services deal end China's hallyu ban? Not quite
item.description:
Did China just lift its ban on Korean culture?

South Korea and China announced on Nov. 18, at a summit in Shenzhen held alongside the APEC leaders' meeting, that they had substantially concluded the services and investment follow-up to their 2015 free trade agreement. Talks began in March 2018, eight years and eight months ago. "Substantially concluded" means negotiations are over, with some technical wording still to be settled by working-level officials.

Korean headlines quickly called it the end of China's informal ban on Korean pop culture. The government's press release never uses that phrase. What it records are two commitments: China will give Korean films, games and similar content most-favored-nation treatment, and it will apply a non-discrimination principle when screening online games, films and other content before release.

Most-favored nation is not a fast lane

Most-favored-nation treatment means China cannot treat Korean content worse than content from any other country. If Beijing clears a foreign game with a short review, it has to apply the same standard to a Korean one. It does not mean Korean titles get approved first, or at all.

Likewise, applying non-discrimination to pre-release screening means the screening itself stays. Seoul says this is the first time China has written such commitments into a trade agreement, which would let Seoul raise any breach under the agreement once it is in force. The deal also widens co-production beyond film, the only format in the 2015 agreement, to TV dramas, animation, variety shows and documentaries.

Tour operators, stores, builders and law firms

Korean travel agencies set up in 23 Chinese regions will be allowed to sell overseas trips to people living in China, a business the 2015 agreement did not cover. China was Korea's largest source of visitors in 2025, at 5.48 million, or 28.9% of the total, and each spent $1,504 on average, 13% above the overall figure. That works out to roughly $8.2 billion in total spending.

Korean retailers will be able to run 30 or more stores in China without a Chinese joint-venture partner. The deal removes the 2015 limits that confined Korean builders to five types of projects. Korean law firms that partner with Chinese firms will be able to set up in Tianjin, Qianhai and Hainan as well as Shanghai. In finance, Korea automatically gets any wider financial-market access China later promises another country in a trade agreement. Korea, for its part, opened law-firm tie-ups, construction-equipment rental and film screening to Chinese firms.

On investment, neither side may require technology transfer as a condition. The market-opening schedule switches to a negative list, under which everything not listed is open, and a ratchet clause stops either government from tightening a rule once it has loosened it. Investor-state arbitration now also covers the pre-establishment stage, such as an arbitrary refusal of permits before a project starts.

Goods 20.7%, services 12.4%

China accounted for $272.9 billion, or 20.7%, of Korea's $1.3154 trillion in goods trade in 2024, but only $38.8 billion, or 12.4%, of its $313.5 billion in services trade. If China's share of services matched its share of goods, the figure would be about $64.9 billion, or $26.1 billion more than in 2024.

Expectations need tempering, though. The press release's own figures show two-way goods trade at $228.9 billion in 2013, before the original deal took effect, $240 billion in 2017 and $272.7 billion in 2025, a 19% increase over 12 years. Those figures alone cannot isolate the deal's effect.

When does any of this take effect?

None of this is in effect yet. The trade ministry will finish a legal review of the text, then move to a formal signing and entry into force. Under Korea's constitution, a trade treaty of this kind needs the National Assembly's consent.

The 2015 agreement offers a guide: substantially concluded in November 2014, signed on June 1, 2015, and in force on Dec. 20, 2015, about 13 months in all. Content, travel and retail companies planning a move into China should assume current rules apply until the new deal is in force.

item.title: The same 12.5% Section 301 tariff costs Korean goods less than Vietnamese ones
item.description:
The decision

The US Trade Representative began imposing Section 301 duties on goods from dozens of economies on July 24, 2026, after investigations found they had failed to ban or effectively block imports made with forced labor. The notice ran in the Federal Register on July 28.

South Korea got a "12.5% net of MFN" rate. If a product's duty rate is below 12.5%, the Section 301 duty tops it up to a combined 12.5%. If the rate is 12.5% or more, the Section 301 duty is zero. Japan and Switzerland are treated the same way.

Vietnam, Thailand and the Philippines are not. Their goods pay 12.5% on top of the regular rate. The EU and Taiwan are topped up to 10%. The US tariff schedule spells this out in Chapter 99: for Korea, heading 9903.05.71 (rate below 12.5%) reads "12.5%" and 9903.05.70 (12.5% or more) leaves the duty unchanged; heading 9903.05.84 for Vietnam reads "the duty provided in the applicable subheading + 12.5%".

Three products, worked through

Cosmetics under HTS 3304.99.50 carry no regular duty, so goods from Korea, Japan, Vietnam and Thailand all pay 12.5% and goods from the EU and Taiwan pay 10%. Origin matters little here.

Instant noodles and similar pasta under 1902.30.00 carry a 6.4% regular rate. From Korea or Japan the total is 12.5%; from Vietnam or Thailand it is 18.9%. On a $10,000 shipment, that is $1,250 in duty from Korea and $1,890 from Vietnam. That is for Korean noodles entered without a KORUS claim; what a claim changes is covered below.

Cotton sweaters under 6110.20.20 carry a 16.5% regular rate. Because that is above 12.5%, sweaters from Korea, Japan, the EU and Taiwan pay no Section 301 duty and stay at 16.5%; from Vietnam or Thailand the total is 29%. On $10,000 of sweaters, that is $1,650 from Korea against $2,900 from Vietnam. Japan has no US preferential rate on this line.

Does a KORUS claim lower it further?

Korean cotton sweaters and instant noodles are duty-free under the US-Korea free trade agreement (KORUS) if they meet its origin rules. How Section 301 applies once that claim is made is not spelled out consistently. The Chapter 99 headings for Korea and the new U.S. note 52 measure the cap against the "column 1" rate, and the notice separately sets out how to convert properly claimed column 1-Special rates for Korean goods; read that way, a KORUS claim takes the base to zero and Section 301 tops it up to 12.5%. The notice's main text, however, refers to the MFN rate, which would put the sweater under 9903.05.70 with no Section 301 duty and leave only the KORUS rate of zero. On that reading, KORUS-claimed noodles would pay only the 6.1% Section 301 duty measured against their 6.4% regular rate. CBP's July 23 guidance (CSMS #69326983) does not address the point. Confirm with CBP or a licensed customs broker before relying on either reading.

Not everything is covered. Excluded are articles of steel, aluminum and copper; passenger vehicles, light trucks, medium- and heavy-duty vehicles and their parts; wood products; semiconductors; articles for pharmaceutical use; civil aircraft parts; and certain minerals and raw materials listed in the annexes. The exemptions sit in the notice's annexes and in Chapter 99 headings 9903.05.85 to 9903.05.92. The three products above are assumed not to be exempt, and the EU and Taiwan have country-specific exemption lists of their own.

Korean export numbers

Korea Customs Service data show South Korea's cosmetics exports to the US at $2.049 billion in January–October 2026, up 37.6% from a year earlier, and exports of instant noodles and similar pasta at $325 million, up 30.9%. The figures include three months of shipments made after the duty took effect, but export data cannot show whether the duty changed demand.

Before any KORUS claim, for products with a regular rate below 12.5%, the Korea–Vietnam gap equals that regular rate; at 12.5% or above, the gap is 12.5 points. For Korean exporters pitching US buyers, the product's US regular rate now feeds directly into the price comparison; whether a KORUS claim lowers it further needs confirming with CBP.

item.title: Oil prices are falling. Why South Korea's gas price cap hasn't moved
item.description:
Why the pump price hasn't budged

Oil has come down since October, yet the price board at a South Korean gas station has barely changed. On November 17 the national average for gasoline was 1,854.77 won a litre, according to Opinet, the price tracker run by the state-owned Korea National Oil Corporation. That is about $1.39 a litre, or roughly $5.26 a gallon. Diesel averaged 1,841.58 won. A week earlier gasoline was 1,855.13 won.

The reason is a price cap. Since March 13, after war in the Middle East sent fuel prices soaring, the government has used Article 23 of the Petroleum and Alternative Fuel Business Act to set a ceiling on what refiners may charge gas stations. The ceiling is 1,784 won a litre for gasoline, 1,773 won for diesel and 1,380 won for kerosene. On November 13 the Ministry of Trade, Industry and Resources said the 12th round of the cap would keep those levels for four weeks from November 14.

The cap applies to what refiners charge, not to what drivers pay. Stations add their own costs and margin on top, which is why the average pump price sits about 71 won above the cap for gasoline and about 69 won above it for diesel. As long as the ceiling holds, pump prices have little room to move.

Crude is still dearer than when the cap was set

The 1,784-won level dates from the seventh round on June 27, when the ministry cut the cap by 150 won from 1,934 won. The United States and Iran had just agreed a memorandum of understanding to end the war, and Brent had dropped to $72 a barrel on June 26.

Prices climbed again. Ministry figures put Brent at an average of $84 in July, $105.8 on September 16 and an average of $108 in October, before it eased to $96 on November 12. That is still 33% above the level when the cap was set. Shipping costs have soared as well: a tanker freight index for the Middle East-to-China route rose from 225 on February 27 and 295 on June 26 to 1,202 on November 6, more than fourfold since the cap was set. The ministry blames attacks on ships near the Strait of Hormuz.

On November 13 the ministry acknowledged that crude and shipping costs remain high, but said it would hold the cap to keep prices stable for households. The ceiling has now stood at 1,784 won for six rounds in a row.

Who pays when costs top the cap

When crude costs rise but refiners cannot pass them on, refiners lose money. The same Article 23 lets the government compensate refiners, importers and fuel sellers for losses caused by a price ceiling. The ministry proposed rules for doing so in June and has since finalized them.

Compensation is based on cost: what a refiner spent buying and shipping crude, plus refining and selling it, with room for a reasonable margin. Claims are settled quarterly and must be filed within 60 days of a quarter's end, extendable by 30 days. The first period ran from March 13 to June 30. A settlement committee of up to 20 accounting, legal and oil-market experts and government officials has been operating since July.

The industry's arithmetic is different: it puts refiners' cumulative losses at 5 trillion won (about $3.7 billion). In a September 16 statement the ministry rejected that figure, saying it appears to be based on international product prices, and said it had made clear from the start that compensation would be based on costs. The ministry has not said how much it has paid.

What eight months of the cap have done

By one official estimate, the cap has kept inflation lower. The ministry cites a November 12 analysis by the Korea Development Institute, a state-funded think tank, estimating that from March to October the cap lowered annual fuel-price inflation by an average of about 12 percentage points a month, and overall consumer price inflation by about 0.6 points.

Critics argued that capping prices would push up fuel consumption. Ministry data do not show that: from the second week of March through August, station sales were down 2.1% for gasoline and 8.4% for diesel from a year earlier. The ministry says gasoline sales fell less than diesel because drivers have been switching from diesel cars to gasoline and hybrid models.

Other countries are holding prices down too. Japan has used subsidies since April to keep gasoline below 170 yen a litre and diesel below 160 yen, the ministry said in September. South Korea instead caps what refiners charge stations and settles with refiners afterwards.

What it means for a driver

Take a gasoline car that does 12 km a litre (about 28 miles per gallon) and is driven 1,000 km a month. It burns about 83.3 litres, which at today's average costs roughly 154,600 won, or about $116, a month.

If the cap moved by 150 won, as it did in June, and pump prices followed, that same driver's monthly bill would change by about 12,500 won ($9), or about 150,000 won ($112) a year. On February 28, before prices spiked, gasoline averaged 1,692.89 won. Today's price is 161.88 won, or 9.6%, higher.

The next decision comes in December

The 12th round runs through December 11. The ministry reviews the cap every four weeks but has said it may adjust the four-week cycle as conditions in the Middle East and oil markets change. If crude keeps falling it can lower the cap, as it did in June; if prices rise it can raise it, as it did in the second round.

The ministry has said the cap will end once the war ends, shipping through the Strait of Hormuz returns to normal and crude settles in the $90s, according to several Korean news outlets. On November 12 Dubai crude was $90 and Brent $96, so only the price condition is close; the ministry said on November 13 that ships near the Strait of Hormuz were still being attacked. Whether the cap continues into 2027 has not been decided.

Taxpayers foot the bill. Originally expecting the cap to last six months, the government set aside a 4.2 trillion won ($3.1 billion) contingency reserve for losses from March to September, then put another 1.45 trillion won ($1.09 billion), covering October to December of this year, into its 2027 budget proposal, according to several Korean outlets: about 5.65 trillion won ($4.2 billion) in all. These are budgeted sums, not payments. Refiners are expected to be told between late November and early December how much they will get for March 13 to June 30.

item.title: Chinese hot-rolled steel imports to South Korea fell 77% after anti-dumping duties, and Japan now supplies 65%
item.description:
A new map for Korea's hot-rolled imports

If you sell steel into South Korea, the question since Seoul started imposing anti-dumping duties is simple: where did the orders go? Korea Customs Service import data for January–October 2026 give a clear answer for hot-rolled steel, the coil that feeds car parts, construction and pipe mills. The figures below leave out heavy plate.

Imports from China fell 76.7%, from 1,215,000 tonnes to 283,000 tonnes. Imports from Japan rose 13.2%, from 1,004,000 to 1,137,000 tonnes. Taiwan went from 51,000 to 187,000 tonnes, 3.7 times as much, and Vietnam from 15,000 to 123,000 tonnes, 8.1 times as much. Total hot-rolled imports fell 23.4%, from 2.29 million to 1.75 million tonnes. These figures cover HS 7208 only. We also checked the alloy-steel hot-rolled codes the duty covers (under HS 7225.30, 7225.40, 7226.20 and 7226.91): imports from China fell 72.9%, from 69,000 to 19,000 tonnes, so Chinese shipments did not shift there.

In short, while Chinese imports fell by 932,000 tonnes, imports from Japan, Taiwan and Vietnam together rose by about 377,000 tonnes, and total imports fell by about 536,000 tonnes. Changes in Korean demand could also play a part; the trade data cannot separate the two. China's share of Korea's hot-rolled imports dropped from 53.1% to 16.1%; Japan's rose from 43.8% to 64.8%.

Same duties, different timing

In Korea, the Korea Trade Commission investigates dumping and recommends duties, and the finance ministry imposes them by ministerial ordinance. The rates for the two countries are close. Provisional duties started on Sept. 23, 2025, and were extended to nine months, through June 22, 2026; the next day an ordinance made them definitive for five years on June 23, 2026: 31.58% to 33.43% for Japanese suppliers and 28.16% to 33.10% for Chinese ones.

Both countries' biggest mills can avoid the duty. The same ordinance exempts suppliers that agreed to sell at or above a minimum price, known as price undertakings. On the Japanese side that covers JFE Steel, Nippon Steel and Tokyo Steel and the trading houses that export their coil, including Korean-owned traders such as SeAH Japan and POSCO International Japan. On the Chinese side it covers big mills including Baoshan Iron & Steel, Angang, Shougang and Shagang, shipping through designated exporters. The floor is reset every quarter based on Chinese and Japanese domestic prices and the won-dollar exchange rate. The undertakings took effect with the definitive duties on June 23, 2026.

Splitting the year at that date tells a sharper story. In January–May, before the definitive duties and the undertakings took effect, Japanese hot-rolled imports slipped 4.4%, from 588,000 to 562,000 tonnes, and Chinese imports were just 15,000 tonnes, down from 740,000. Taiwan (from 1,000 to 105,000 tonnes) and Vietnam (from 2,000 to 58,000 tonnes) grew fastest but replaced only a fraction. From June to October (the undertakings applied from June 23), Japanese imports jumped 38.1%, from 417,000 to 575,000 tonnes, and 268,000 tonnes came in from China, against 475,000 a year earlier. The timing lines up, but customs data do not show which shipments entered under an undertaking, so they cannot prove the exemptions caused the rebound.

Prices swapped places. Japanese hot-rolled coil averaged $531 a tonne, up 2.4% from $519; Chinese coil rose 15.8%, from $489 to $566. A year ago Chinese coil landed about $30 a tonne below Japanese; in January–October 2026 it averaged about $35 above it. Average unit values also move when the product mix changes, so treat them as a guide rather than a quote.

Cold-rolled coil and slab, outside the duties

Chinese products not covered by anti-dumping duties grew. Cold-rolled coil, hot-rolled coil rolled thinner again at room temperature, rose 58.1% from 389,000 to 615,000 tonnes; China supplies 95.5% of Korea's cold-rolled imports, although Korea's total cold-rolled imports also rose 63.4%. Semi-finished steel such as slab and billet from China rose 88.4%, from 318,000 to 599,000 tonnes, but Japanese semis fell 14.1%, from 706,000 to 606,000 tonnes, so Korea's total semi-finished imports grew only 7.9%. Slab is the feedstock rolling mills turn into hot-rolled coil and plate; the data do not show who bought it or what it became.

A year earlier Chinese cold-rolled coil cost $585 a tonne, 20% more than Chinese hot-rolled at $489. In January–October 2026 it averaged $567, almost exactly the $566 for hot-rolled, mostly because Chinese hot-rolled got dearer. Against the average for all imported hot-rolled coil, which rose from $504 to $538, the cold-rolled premium narrowed from 16% to 5%.

Zinc-coated steel took a different path. In April 2026 the Trade Commission recommended provisional duties of 22.34% to 33.67% on Chinese galvanized cold-rolled steel thinner than 4.75 mm. Imports of Chinese coated flat steel fell from a monthly average of 159,000 tonnes in January–May to 14,000 tonnes in July, then climbed back to 52,000 tonnes in September and 42,000 in October. For January–October as a whole they fell 30.3%, from 1.41 million to 980,000 tonnes. This customs category mixes covered and uncovered products, so the data alone cannot say which kind came back. Vietnamese coated flat steel rose from 326 tonnes to 26,760 tonnes, still small next to China.

What could be blocked next

On Oct. 23 the Trade Commission recommended five-year duties of 22.34% to 33.67% on Chinese galvanized cold-rolled steel, with price undertakings for 10 exporters. The finance minister has yet to decide. On Sept. 17 it recommended provisional duties of 25.08% to 27.96% on Chinese steel bar, and on Oct. 8 it opened a case on Chinese seamless pipe, with a preliminary ruling due in February 2027.

Korea has also widened its anti-circumvention rules. The enforcement decree of the Customs Act, the presidential decree that sets out how the law is applied, was amended on Nov. 28, 2025, to treat changing the shape, form or use of a dutied product without changing its essential character as circumvention, even if the tariff code changes. Simple assembly or processing in a third country of materials from the dutied supplier country also counts. If the Trade Commission finds circumvention, the same duty can be extended to those goods. The trade data do not show whether any of the cold-rolled or slab imports would meet that test; the decree's list does not cover processing inside Korea, such as rolling imported slab in a Korean mill.

For suppliers, access to the Korean market now turns less on the headline duty rate than on price undertakings and where the product lines are drawn. For Korean mills, imported hot-rolled coil has become scarcer and Chinese coil dearer since the duties took effect, while duty-free cold-rolled and slab imports grew over the same period. The country-by-product figures here can be updated when final November data come out in mid-December; the Nov. 1–20 preliminary figures due at 9 a.m. Seoul time on Nov. 23 (7 p.m. Nov. 22 in New York) do not break out countries or products.

item.title: Brazil, Australia and Spain gain share of Korea's chicken, beef and pork imports
item.description:
Chicken: Brazil's share climbs to 80%

Brazil supplied 79.8% of the $618 million of chicken cuts (HS 020714) South Korea imported in the 12 months to October 2026, according to our calculations from Korea Customs Service data. A year earlier, in the 12 months to October 2025, its share was 71.1%. Thailand's share fell from 24.7% to 15.6%. These shares are of imports only, not of total consumption including domestic meat.

The earlier 12 months include events from spring 2025. In May that year a highly pathogenic bird flu outbreak on a Brazilian poultry farm led Seoul to halt imports of Brazilian chicken, and the agriculture ministry moved to let in meat from disease-free areas of Brazil, a process known as regionalization. The suspension fell inside the earlier 12-month period, and total imports of this line rose 20.1% by weight. Brazil's volume rose 27.8%, from 158,000 tonnes to 202,000, while Thailand's fell 18.9%, from 39,000 tonnes to 32,000.

Brazil's price per kilogram rose 18.5%, from $2.06 to $2.44, yet it was still about 20% cheaper than Thai chicken at $3.04. Thailand shipped $104 million of cooked chicken under another code, more than the $97 million in this line, so this line alone does not show its whole position in Korea.

Duty-free US beef loses ground

Korea's tariff on US beef fell to zero on Jan. 1, 2026, the last step of the phase-out under the Korea-US Free Trade Agreement. Yet the US share of Korea's frozen boneless beef imports (HS 020230) slipped from 36.4% to 33.5% by value, while Australia's rose from 57.3% to 62.2%. Australian volume grew 9.2%, from 143,000 tonnes to 157,000; US volume edged up 1.5%, from 79,000 tonnes to 80,000.

Australian beef got pricier too: $7.64 a kilogram, up 17.7% from $6.49, against $8.02 for US beef, up 7.4% from $7.46. The US premium narrowed from 15% to 5%.

Australia still faces a tariff and a volume cap. Under its own trade agreement with Korea, Australian beef paid 5.3% in 2026, according to the Australian livestock outlet Beef Central and the food-market publication Foodmarket, but the safeguard volume of about 196,000 tonnes was used up in July, triggering a 24% rate for the rest of the year. US beef, duty-free all year, already held a tariff edge; from late July the gap widened to 24 percentage points. The latest 12 months still include Australian beef that cleared before the cap was reached. Declared customs values exclude duty, so the tariff gap does not show up in the per-kilogram prices. The in-quota rate drops to 2.6% in January 2027. In chilled beef (HS 020130), the US held 70.2%, little changed from 69.3%.

Pork: Spain gains with a higher average price

Frozen pork (HS 020329) tells a different story. Spanish volume jumped 62.6%, from 98,000 tonnes to 159,000, lifting its share of import value from 22.3% to 28.1%. US volume fell 2.7%, from 175,000 tonnes to 170,000, and its share dropped from 31.8% to 26.9%. Total frozen pork imports rose 18.7% by weight.

Spain was not the cheaper supplier. Its average fell 10%, from $3.93 a kilogram to $3.54, but that was still 12% above the US average of $3.17. This code lumps together cuts from belly to shoulder and ribs, so the gap may reflect a different mix of cuts rather than a higher price for the same product. Disease controls may also have played a part. After African swine fever was found in wild boar near Barcelona in late November 2025, Japan suspended all imports of Spanish pork, while Korea blocked only meat from the affected area, according to Korean press reports. Some Spanish supply may have shifted to Korea as a result, but the trade data cannot confirm it.

What meat suppliers should watch

In none of the three lines does price alone explain the shift in share. Chicken follows a ban and its lifting; in beef, the US tariff cut did not stop Australia gaining; in pork, the gap may reflect a different mix of cuts. Before benchmarking a per-kilogram price against a rival, check whether the same HS code is hiding different cuts or levels of processing.

What Korea buys from each country, and at what price, is updated monthly on our Korea Trade country pages and the Sell to Korea page. The next preliminary trade figures, for Nov. 1-20, come out at 9 a.m. Korean time on Monday, Nov. 23 (7 p.m. Sunday in New York).

item.title: Korea's main mortgage rate index hits 3.62%, its highest in two years and eight months
item.description:
A rate notice in the banking app

Homeowners in South Korea with variable-rate mortgages may be getting rate-change notices this week. On November 16 the Korea Federation of Banks reported that the new-funds COFIX, the most widely used benchmark for those loans, rose to 3.62% for October. That is up 0.19 percentage points from September, 0.44 points from August, and the highest since February 2024.

But the federation published three versions of COFIX that afternoon, and they did not agree. The balance-based index came in at 3.26%. The new balance index, the third version, was 2.93%. Same name, 0.69 points apart. Which one a loan is tied to decides how much this week's news matters to the borrower.

What COFIX measures, and why there are three

COFIX, short for cost of funds index, is what eight Korean banks pay for the money they lend out: a weighted average of rates on time deposits, installment savings, bank bonds and similar funding. The eight are Shinhan, Woori, SC First, Hana, KB Kookmin, Citibank Korea, NongHyup and IBK. Each bank sets a loan rate by adding its own margin on top.

The versions differ in what they average. The new-funds index covers only money raised that month, so it moves almost as soon as deposit rates do. The balance-based index averages everything on the books at month end, including deposits taken years ago at the rates of the time, so it moves slowly.

The new balance index, introduced in 2019, adds lower-cost money such as settlement balances and other borrowings. That usually keeps it the lowest of the three, and the slowest to move.

A gap that has flipped

We lined up three years of the federation's monthly data. The 0.69-point gap between the new-funds and new balance indexes in October is the widest since January 2023, when it was 0.80.

A year earlier it ran the other way. From April to August 2025 the new-funds index ran below the new balance index; in August it was 2.49%, against 2.54%, because new money gets cheaper first when rates fall. Since then the new-funds index has climbed 1.13 points in 14 months, while over the same 14 months the new balance index rose 0.39 points, from 2.54% to 2.93%.

In money terms, on a 300 million won loan (about $225,000), 0.69 points is 2.07 million won a year in interest, about 172,500 won ($129) a month, if the bank margin were the same. In practice banks can set a different margin for each index, and paying down principal shrinks the balance, so the gap in actual payments is usually smaller.

When the higher rate actually lands

Korean variable-rate loans usually reset every six or 12 months. On the reset date the bank takes the latest published index and adds the margin fixed in the original contract. So a rise in COFIX does not hit a borrower right away; it arrives all at once on their reset date.

Take a six-month loan tied to the new-funds index that last reset in May, after the May 15 release, at 2.89%. If its November reset falls after November 16, it gets 3.62%, a jump of 0.73 points. On 300 million won that adds 2.19 million won a year, about 182,500 won ($137) a month.
