Over the same six months the new balance index rose from 2.49% to 2.93%, or 0.44 points: about 110,000 won ($82) a month on the same loan. Neither index is always cheaper; it depends on which way rates are moving.

Korean borrowers can find which index their loan follows, and how often it resets, in the loan agreement or in the loan details screen of their bank app.

Switching to a fixed rate has its own costs

Several Korean outlets have reported that at some banks, variable mortgage rates are now above fixed-rate offers. Fixed rates track market rates such as bank bond yields, while variable rates track COFIX, so the two can drift apart.

Moving to another bank or a new product means taking out a new loan. That can trigger an early repayment fee, and the borrower's limit is reassessed against current income and lending rules. A fixed rate also stays put if rates later fall. Whether a switch pays depends on the time left on the loan and the size of the rate gap after fees. Some loans allow a switch between rate types with the same bank; the loan agreement or the bank can confirm.

What to watch next

The short-term COFIX, a weekly index based on three-month funding, was 3.50% on November 11; the next reading is due November 18. November's three monthly indexes will be published on December 15.

COFIX is an average across eight banks. Margins and discounts vary by bank, so two borrowers on the same index can pay different rates. The calculator below looks at interest only, before principal repayment and discounts.

item.title: South Korea set to top $1 trillion in exports, decades after selling chipmunks
item.description:
Days away from a first

South Korea had exported $963.7 billion of goods this year by Nov. 10, combining final customs data through October with preliminary figures for early November, leaving about $36.3 billion to go. In Nov. 1-10 it shipped an average of $4.46 billion per working day. If that pace holds, exports would reach $997.1 billion by Nov. 19 and $1.0016 trillion by Nov. 20, according to calculations reported by Korean media.

That would make South Korea only the fourth country to export more than $1 trillion of goods in a year, after the United States and Germany (both in 2006) and China (2007). Japan's best year was 2011, at about $790 billion. Until the customs tally confirms it, the milestone remains a projection.

Per person, close to Germany

Divided by South Korea's 51.7 million people (World Bank, 2025), $1 trillion comes to about $19,300 of exports per person. On the same World Bank basis for 2025, Germany exported about $18,300 per person, the United States $6,400, Japan $5,900 and China $2,700; South Korea's own 2025 figure, on customs data ($709.3 billion), was $13,700. The years differ, so this is only a rough comparison, but at $1 trillion South Korea's exports per head would be close to Germany's 2025 level. Smaller trading hubs such as the Netherlands export far more per person, over $40,000.

Chipmunks at a dollar each

In 1961, according to a Statistics Korea retrospective, the country's biggest export was iron ore. Four of its ten largest exports were minerals such as tungsten, anthracite and graphite; the only factory-made product on the list was plywood. Almost anything that could be caught or dug up was sold abroad, from lugworms and snakes to grasshoppers and eels.

Wild Siberian chipmunks, small striped squirrels native to Korea, were shipped to Japan as pets from 1962 at $1 each. By 1970 Korea was exporting 300,000 a year, with traders advancing money to farm households near the Taebaek Mountains to catch them, until fears for the wild population led to a cap of 100,000 a year. It was not only chipmunks: in 1976 alone, Korea exported $2 million of toothpicks made from Gangwon Province birch, at $7 per 10,000.

Exports first passed $100 million on Nov. 30, 1964, a date the government marked as Export Day, the origin of today's Trade Day. The year's total was $119 million.

A tank in every public toilet

In the 1970s, wigs made from human hair were among the country's main exports. Public toilets carried white plastic tanks and signs reading 'Your urine earns precious foreign currency.' The urine was processed into urokinase, an enzyme used as a clot-dissolving drug, and sold abroad. Statistics Korea says a kilogram fetched more than $2,000.

Then and now, in the same numbers

At early November's pace of $4.46 billion per working day, South Korea now ships the equivalent of its entire 1964 exports ($119 million) in about 38 minutes, if a working day's exports are spread evenly over 24 hours. Measured by calendar days, weekends included, it is about 51 minutes.

Integrated circuits (HS 8542), the country's biggest export today, averaged $22,756 a kilogram in October 2026, roughly 11 times the urokinase price in nominal dollars. Adjusted with the US consumer price index, a 1970s dollar is worth $4.60 to $8.70 today, so $2,000 then is roughly $9,300 to $17,400 now. Chips still come out 1.3 to 2.4 times as valuable per kilogram.

The early jumps came fast: seven years from $100 million to $1 billion, then six more to $10 billion. After that the gaps stretched to 18 years for $100 billion and, if this week's projection holds, 31 for $1 trillion. World Bank data put the same $100 billion-to-$1 trillion climb at 31 years for the United States (1975-2006), 30 for Germany (1976-2006) and 13 for China (1994-2007), so South Korea's climb, 31 years from 1995 to the projected 2026 mark, took about as long as those of the US and Germany, though in nominal dollars over different decades.

When the government set a $10 billion export target around 1972, textiles, steel and electronics led exports. In 1976 Hyundai shipped five Pony cars to Ecuador, the country's first official car exports. When exports passed $100 billion in 1995, the top three were chips, cars and ships.

What the trillion rests on

Preliminary customs data show chips accounted for $16.6 billion, or 49.7%, of the $33.5 billion exported in Nov. 1-10, up 331.2% from the same period a year earlier, a ten-day figure that can swing sharply. For the year to Nov. 10 the chip share is about 43% (roughly $415 billion on preliminary figures). Both shares use the customs office's broader 'semiconductors' grouping, not HS 8542 alone. By one Korean newspaper's count, chips account for 74.3% of this year's export growth.

Final customs data put the trade surplus for January to October at $295.0 billion, 3.8 times last year's full-year surplus of $77.4 billion. The surplus with the United States alone was $102.3 billion (exports $176.8 billion, imports $74.5 billion), about a third of the total. With chips making up such a large share, a turn in the chip cycle could hit the export total hard.

What comes next

The customs service will publish preliminary figures for Nov. 1-20 at 9 a.m. Korean time on Monday, Nov. 23 (7 p.m. Sunday in New York), because the 21st falls on a Saturday. That release should show whether the $1 trillion mark was crossed; if not, confirmation waits for the trade ministry's full-month report on Dec. 1. For product-by-product and country-by-country data, see our Korea Trade pages.

item.title: Container freight from the US to South Korea now costs a quarter of the outbound rate or less
item.description:
A quarter of the price or less, inbound

If you ship goods from the United States or Europe to South Korea, your freight bill is likely to be far lower than for the same box going the other way, and the gap has widened sharply this year. The Korea Customs Service publishes average freight charges from import and export declarations. In October 2026, a 40-foot container from the US West Coast to Korea cost 24% of the Korea-to-West Coast rate. From the US East Coast it was 16%, and from the European Union 17%.

A year earlier the two directions were much closer: 92% on the West Coast lane, 62% on the East Coast and 31% for the EU. Between October 2025 and October 2026, the Korea-to-West Coast rate rose 82.3% and the West Coast-to-Korea rate fell 52.0%. On the East Coast lane, the rates rose 84.9% and fell 51.8%. Rates moved sharply in both directions, which together drove the gap.

The customs service does not publish the unit behind these averages, so we compare only the two directions within the same data set, and their changes, rather than quoting dollar amounts. Its Korea-to-West Coast figure is the same for September and October. Actual quotes vary by carrier and forwarder.

A lopsided lane, and not a new one

Korean port data show how lopsided the lane is. From October 2025 to September 2026, 1.72 million TEU (twenty-foot equivalent units) of containers arrived at Korean ports from the United States, according to the Ministry of Oceans and Fisheries, and 598,000 TEU of them, or 34.8%, were empty. Over the same months 2.57 million TEU left Korean ports for the US, only 0.4% of them empty. These are port figures, so they may include cargo transshipped through Busan, Korea's main port and a regional hub, on its way to other countries.

Put another way, for every 100 loaded containers leaving Korean ports for the US, only 44 loaded ones arrive from there. Carriers typically send the rest back empty so they can be loaded with the next export cargo. On a return, or 'backhaul', leg like this, lines usually prefer to fill space cheaply rather than sail it empty, which tends to keep inbound rates low.

But the imbalance is not new. From October 2024 to September 2025, 39.4% of containers arriving from the US were empty, and 46 loaded boxes came in for every 100 that went out, yet in October 2025 the West Coast rate ratio was still 92%. Empties alone cannot explain why the gap widened this year. Outbound volumes have grown: in September 2026, 243,000 TEU left Korean ports for the US, 21.6% more than the 200,000 TEU a year earlier, while loaded containers arriving from the US held roughly steady at 93,000 TEU against 91,000. That fits with the rise in outbound rates, but the freight and port figures cannot show the cause on their own.

Each lane tells a different story

Mexico is the extreme case: 72% of containers arriving in Korea from Mexico were empty, and for every 100 loaded boxes leaving Korean ports for Mexico, about eight loaded ones came in. Taiwan (39%), Spain (37%) and the United Kingdom (34%) also send back many empties.

Japan shows that empties do not set the price by themselves. Some 41% of boxes from Japan arrive empty, yet the Japan-to-Korea rate was 2.2 times the Korea-to-Japan rate in October 2026, and loaded flows are close to even, at 92 in for every 100 out.

China runs the other way. Only 3% of containers arriving from China were empty, while 47.7% of those leaving Korean ports for China were. Rates flip too: in October 2026 the China-to-Korea rate was 3.7 times the Korea-to-China rate. Vietnam is close to balanced, with about 5% empties in each direction, and its Korea-bound rate was 78% of the outbound one.

What to check in a quote

The import averages come from declarations on FOB terms, where freight is billed separately, and the export averages from CIF and CFR declarations, where freight is built into the price and split out on the form. Because the two are recorded differently, the ratio between them may lean one way. Both cover full-container-load shipments in standard 40-foot dry containers, so less-than-container loads and refrigerated boxes may differ.

Even so, the direction gap gives a benchmark. A Korea-bound quote close to the outbound rate on the same lane is worth questioning. Monthly freight and container data by country are on our Korea Trade freight and country pages. The next preliminary export figures, for Nov. 1-20, come out at 9 a.m. Korean time on Monday, Nov. 23 (7 p.m. Sunday in New York).

item.title: South Korea loan sharks: loans above 60% interest are void, and victims can now seek help online
item.description:
Help without a visit

South Korea's financial regulator has moved its help desk for illegal-loan victims online. From November 16, people trapped by unlicensed lenders can apply through the website and app of the Credit Counseling and Recovery Service, a state-backed debt-relief agency, at any hour, the Financial Services Commission said.

Until now, victims had to walk into one of 22 government microfinance centers to be assigned a caseworker. That kept out people who work during the day, live far from a center, or are afraid to go out because collectors are harassing them.

Online applicants get the same free service: a caseworker who tells the lender to stop collecting and close the debt, a free lawyer to handle further contact, a certificate that the loan is void, police referral, and links to debt restructuring and welfare support.

The math that decides what you owe

Korean law measures a loan's cost as simple interest converted to a yearly rate. The formula: interest, divided by the money actually received, times 365, divided by the number of days.

The commission's own example: borrow 300,000 won (about $225) and repay 500,000 won a week later. That is 200,000 won of interest in seven days, or about 3,476% a year.

A more ordinary case: borrow 1 million won ($749) and repay 1.1 million won 30 days later. It looks like 10% for the month, but it works out to about 122% a year, double the 60% line. Put the other way, a 30-day, 1 million won loan crosses 60% once the interest tops about 49,000 won ($37).

Money taken off the top does not count as money lent. If a lender advertises 1 million won but hands over 900,000 won after taking 100,000 won off the top, the law treats 900,000 won as the loan. Repaying 1 million won in 30 days then comes to about 135% a year. Fees, commissions and other charges tied to the loan are all counted as interest; only a few costs, such as collateral registration and credit checks, are excluded.

Loans dressed up as something else can be measured the same way. In one scheme, a borrower gets 200,000 won in cash and must send 300,000 won worth of gift vouchers 20 days later. That is about 913% a year.

Three lines in the law

Registered lenders may charge at most 20% a year, a cap set by decree below the law's 27.9% ceiling. Anything above that is void, and interest already paid over the cap is credited against the principal, with any surplus refundable.

A 2025 amendment to the money-lending law, in force since July 22 of that year, added a second line. A loan priced above three times the cap, set by decree at 60% a year, is void in its entirety. The borrower owes neither principal nor interest and can reclaim what was paid. Contracts involving sexual exploitation in collection, or extracted through violence or threats on grossly unfair terms, are void in full at any rate.

Unregistered lenders face a third rule: they cannot collect interest at all, even below 60%. Borrowers can check whether a lender is registered through the lender search on FINE, the Financial Supervisory Service's consumer portal.

A certificate that has held up in court

For loans made on or after July 22, 2025, the Financial Supervisory Service, the country's financial watchdog, issues a certificate in its governor's name declaring the contract void. The agency texts the lender, sends the certificate to both sides, and borrowers can use it to refuse payment, sue for refunds, or present it in criminal cases. The state Korea Legal Aid Corporation offers free help with lawsuits.

On September 29, a Daegu court acquitted a borrower whom lenders had accused of fraud after the borrower failed to deliver gift vouchers sold in advance: cash up front, with vouchers worth more due weeks later. According to the commission, the court relied on the certificate to treat the deal as a disguised illegal loan.

Eight months in numbers

Between February 23 and October 31, when the service was in-person only, 987 people reported 7,231 illegal debts, an average of 7.3 each. Caseworkers demanded that lenders stop collecting on 5,469 of them and won agreements to close 776 by the end of October, about one in seven, with some cases possibly still open. Regulators issued 192 void certificates, assigned lawyers in 2,623 cases and referred 1,178 lenders to police.

Lenders do not always comply. One victim, borrowing from new lenders to pay off old ones, ended up owing 9.7 million won ($7,261) to 21 lenders. When none agreed to close the debts, the case moved to lawyers and a void certificate.

What to keep in mind

A self-calculated rate is a guide, not a ruling. Whether a loan is void depends on when it was signed, how much money actually changed hands and whether the lender is registered; disputes go to the regulator and the courts. The void certificate covers only loans made on or after July 22, 2025; older loans are best discussed with a caseworker. Keeping transfer records and chat logs makes the arithmetic possible.

The commission says it will monitor early demand for the online channel. From December, police officers will be stationed at the debt-relief agency so referrals can happen at the counseling stage.

In Korea, victims can report illegal lending to the Financial Supervisory Service at 1332, and people struggling with debt can call the Korea Inclusive Finance Agency at 1397 or the Credit Counseling and Recovery Service at 1375.

item.title: South Korea to let credit card points become local currency from 2027
item.description:
A second way out for card points

Every swipe of a Korean credit card earns reward points, and the balances add up. Card companies hold 2.1 trillion won, about $1.6 billion, in accumulated points, according to the government.

On November 13, the Office for Government Policy Coordination, the interior ministry and the Financial Services Commission presented a plan at a policy coordination meeting chaired by the prime minister: from May 2027, cardholders will be able to turn those points into local currency. They will check their points in AccountInfo, an app run by the Korea Financial Telecommunications and Clearings Institute, or in a local-currency app, choose an amount, and spend it from the next day.

Local currency in Korea means vouchers issued by cities and counties, usually as a prepaid card or app balance, that can be spent at registered shops in that area.

Cash is already on the table

The points can already become cash. Since January 5, 2021, AccountInfo and a lookup service run by the Credit Finance Association, the card industry's trade body, have let cardholders see every card company's points in one place and send them to a bank account. At launch, AccountInfo was open only to Korean nationals, while the association's service also took foreign residents.

Each card company's flagship points convert at one won per point; points tied to partner merchants are excluded. Hyundai Card's M points, which are not one to one, must first be switched into the company's H-Coin.

Between January 5 and the end of May 2021, card companies received 17.99 million cash-out requests worth 203.4 billion won, about $152 million, or roughly 11,300 won ($8) per request.

Voucher conversion is not new either. Korean media report that KB Kookmin Card and NH NongHyup Card already let cardholders convert points into local currency, but only in areas where each has a deal with the voucher operator. The government plan would link many card companies and local currencies through a single gateway, AccountInfo.

What changes when points become vouchers

Local currency falls under the Local Love Gift Certificate Act, the law that governs these city and county vouchers.

By default, vouchers can be spent only inside the issuing city or county, unless a local ordinance says otherwise. Local governments may also refuse to register businesses that are not small or mid-sized, which gives them grounds to keep out big-box stores and department stores. Whether a given shop takes them depends on local rules.

Getting cash back is harder. The law bars users from asking voucher sales agents or shops to cash them out. Once a holder has spent a set share of a voucher's value, the shop must refund the rest on request. The law's implementing decree puts that share between 60% and 80%, and each local ordinance picks the figure. Below that line, the leftover is not refunded but stays spendable.

On a 30,000 won ($22) voucher, that means spending at least 18,000 won ($13) where the threshold is 60%, or 24,000 won ($18) where it is 80%. The plan does not say how this rule will apply to vouchers converted from points. By law, vouchers expire five years after issue, though local governments can shorten or extend that.

Why the government wants a voucher route

The aim is to steer the money to neighborhood shops. The plan follows a June 30 cabinet meeting at which the president ordered officials to turn hidden points into local currency to support traditional markets and small merchants.

The government says it will also talk to public bodies about converting points such as KTX rail mileage and carbon-reduction rewards, and will encourage retailers and airlines to join voluntarily.

What the plan leaves out

The announcement does not say how many won of local currency a point will buy, or whether the discount many cities offer on voucher purchases will apply. Under the law, such discounts are set by each local government.

It also does not say which city's currency points can go into: the holder's home area, or any area they choose. That will decide how useful the option is.

Checking your own points

For now, cardholders can look up their points across all card companies in AccountInfo or the association's service.

Some points still lapse, though less than before. In 2019, before one-app cash-outs existed, 117.1 billion won ($88 million) of the 3.54 trillion won in points earned expired unused, or 3.3%, down from 5.3% in 2015. Card terms let points lapse after five years, and card companies must notify holders every month from six months before.

Points that expire before May 2027 will lapse before the voucher option opens. Until then they can be cashed out or used to pay card bills and purchases.

How the voucher route compares with cash will depend on details not yet announced: the conversion rate, any discount, and which area's currency points can go into.

item.title: Korea's top tax exam scorer admits AI cheating. Is it a crime?
item.description:
What is known, and what isn't

On the morning of November 15, the person who placed first on South Korea's 63rd certified tax accountant exam went on a lawyer's YouTube channel and admitted to cheating on both rounds of this year's test. The candidate, identified only as A, said they photographed the questions with a tiny camera, sent them to a generative AI tool and read the answers off a smartphone. In Korea, certified tax accountants are licensed professionals who prepare tax filings and represent taxpayers before the tax authorities, a profession separate from CPAs. That same day A handed a written confession to the Seoul Metropolitan Police Agency, which assigned the case to its major crimes unit.

Suspicion started with the scores. A missed just one of 160 multiple-choice questions in the first round, according to Korean media, with perfect marks in three of four subjects.

Much is still unverified. The method described so far comes only from A. Whether other test-takers did the same, or whether anyone helped, is for the police to establish.

Can cheating land A in court?

Voiding the exam and a five-year ban, both set out in the tax accountant law, are administrative penalties. Criminal liability is a separate question, and the tax accountant law does not answer it: its penalty clauses cover things like practicing without a license or leaking clients' secrets, not cheating on the exam. Any criminal charge would have to come from the Criminal Act.

Korean media have pointed to two offenses. Article 137 punishes anyone who obstructs a public official's duties by deception, with up to five years in prison or a fine of up to 10 million won (about $7,500). Article 314 punishes obstructing another person's business by deception or force, with up to five years or a fine of up to 15 million won (about $11,200). Korea's Supreme Court has held that obstructing a public official's duties falls under Article 137, not Article 314. The tax exam is held under the finance minister's authority but administered by HRD Korea, a public agency under the labor ministry whose staff are not civil servants. Which charge fits will depend on whose work was disrupted, something the investigation and any trial will have to settle.

A better score obtained unfairly is not automatically a crime. In 1966 the Supreme Court upheld the acquittal of a student who had memorized answers from a copy of the marking scheme handed over by a sister. The student had not obtained the sheet by any wrongful act of their own, the court reasoned, and a candidate who happened to know the answers could not be expected to leave them off the page. What A describes, smuggling in a camera and sending the questions out, is a different situation. Whether it happened that way is for the police to establish.

Turning oneself in counts for something. Article 52 of the Criminal Act lets a court reduce or waive the sentence of someone who turns themselves in to investigators, though it is not obliged to, and whether A's statement to the police counts as surrender is also for the court to decide. And whatever happens in a criminal court, the exam can still be voided and the five-year ban imposed under the tax accountant law.

The law says 'stop' or 'void', not 'revoke'

Cheating on the exam is covered by Article 5-3 of the Certified Tax Accountant Act. It says the minister of finance and economy shall stop or void the exam of anyone who cheats, and shall bar that person from the exam for five years from the date of the decision. The ban is mandatory, not discretionary. Under the act's enforcement decree, that power is delegated to the commissioner of the National Tax Service.

Set that beside Korea's other licensing laws and one difference stands out. Article 5-2 of the Certified Public Accountant Act requires the Financial Services Commission, the financial regulator, to stop the exam or revoke the decision to pass. Article 17 of the Bar Examination Act gives the justice minister the same two options, though its exam ban is discretionary. The tax accountant law does not.

The article says the exam shall be voided, and it does not limit that to cheating caught on the day. What it does not spell out is what happens to a pass that has already been announced once the exam is void. Korean media expect a process to cancel the pass to follow.

The general law also offers a route. Article 18 of the Framework Act on Administrative Affairs lets an agency retroactively cancel an unlawful or improper decision, and where the decision was obtained by deception or other wrongful means, it need not weigh the harm to the person against the public interest first. So the missing word in the tax accountant law does not mean the pass cannot be taken back.

Freeze first, decide later

The finance ministry said on November 15 that it would move quickly, through the Certified Tax Accountant Qualification Review Committee, which sits under the National Tax Service, to suspend the effect of A's certificate and put the pass on hold, Yonhap News Agency reported.

Normally the ministry waits for an investigation to confirm the facts before punishing cheating. This time it said it would act fast because A had confessed. A hold is not a final decision. On November 16 the ministry set up a task force and began proceedings to void the exam and impose the five-year ban the law names; the National Tax Service is holding the required hearing. The ministry also said it would recheck the scores of everyone who passed in the past three to five years and tighten supervision from the 2027 exam.

Does the next person in line get in?

"Top scorer" is not a legal status. The runner-up already passed, so for that person only the ranking changes.

The harder question is for whoever just missed the cut. Under Article 8 of the act's enforcement decree, the second round is passed by scoring at least 40 in every subject and averaging at least 60. If fewer people clear that bar than the minimum number of passes the government sets in advance, the remaining places go to the highest averages.

Say the minimum is 700 and only 500 people average 60 or more. The other 200 places are filled in score order. The question only arises in a year when the minimum had to be topped up this way; if enough people cleared 60 on their own, nobody below the line is affected. If one of those results is voided, 699 people have passed. The decree has no clause for handing the empty place to the next candidate, and the government has not said whether it will.

The accounting exam answers to a different law

A also said the same method was used on the first round of the certified public accountant exam, according to several Korean outlets. That exam falls under the CPA Act, and cheating there is handled by the Financial Services Commission. That law requires a cheat's pass to be revoked, followed by a five-year ban. But the Financial Supervisory Service said on November 15 that A did not pass this year's first round, so there is no pass to revoke.

Passing the tax exam does not by itself let anyone practice. Under Article 6 of the tax accountant act, a new accountant must be entered in the finance ministry's register before taking on clients.

What to watch

First, the police case. The agency that runs the exam, HRD Korea, said it would file a criminal complaint for obstruction of business, and police searched A's home on November 18. Still open: which charges they pursue, and whether the investigation turns up other cheaters or anyone who helped. Second, when the National Tax Service, after its hearing, finalizes voiding A's exam and the ban.

Two questions now sit with the government and the National Assembly: whether to give the tax accountant law a power to revoke a pass, along with rules for the place it leaves empty, and how to keep electronic devices out of exam halls.

item.title: Italy fines Meta €805m over Facebook's photo-gallery access. Why Italy, not Ireland?
item.description:
One tap, the whole gallery

Italy's data protection authority, the Garante, fined Meta Platforms Ireland, the company's EU arm, €805 million (about $889 million) on November 14. The case turns on a single tap: the moment the Facebook app for Android asks for access to your photos and you hit Allow.

The feature at issue is "Get tips from your gallery while browsing Facebook", available since 2023. While you scroll, it surfaces photos and videos from your phone's gallery as ideas for posts. The regulator found three problems. Gallery access was requested through one permission covering the whole app and several features with different purposes. The prompt before it was generic ("enable other features"), so users could not tell they were also agreeing to gallery suggestions. And the feature was switched on by default.

Once granted in full, the Garante said, that kind of permission lets the app read the entire photo library, usually indefinitely, and neither users nor the regulator can check what is actually used. The regulator put the number of people involved at about 20 million Android users in Italy. The investigation began in July 2025 after a complaint from a consumer protection centre in Bolzano.

Why Italy could act without Ireland

Under the EU's General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR), a company operating across the bloc deals mainly with one regulator: the one in the country of its EU headquarters. This "one-stop shop" is why Ireland's Data Protection Commission leads most cases against Meta. Meta argued that Ireland, not Italy, was competent here.

The Garante rejected that. It did not use GDPR. It used Article 122 of Italy's privacy code, which writes into Italian law the EU's ePrivacy Directive, the rule that treats a smartphone as part of a person's private sphere. Under it, any access to information on the device needs free and informed consent, whether or not data leaves the phone and whether or not anyone is harmed. The ePrivacy rules have no one-stop shop, the regulator said, so on a matter involving information on Italian users' phones it could act without going through Ireland.

How the fine was set

The Garante weighed the number of people involved, the fact that the breach is still continuing for users who have not updated the app or have already granted the permission, an earlier 2019 decision against the company, and what it called poor cooperation during the investigation. Changes Meta made after the complaint counted in its favour, but the regulator called them late and limited to people who update the app.

The fine equals about 0.47% of the Meta group's worldwide turnover, roughly 47 cents for every $100 of revenue. Meta has said it disagrees and will appeal, according to multiple reports.

What must change within 60 days

Within 60 days, Meta must ask for consent to this feature on its own, explaining what it is for, that it involves gallery access and how to turn it off. The feature must be off by default, including for people who already granted the permission. If Meta misses the deadline, the feature cannot be switched on for anyone who has not given valid consent. Meta must report its first steps within 30 days and the measures taken within 90 days.

The case did not cover whether photos were used to train AI, which Meta denies. The Garante said it will look separately at a newer feature, launched in 2026, that processes gallery content in the cloud.

How South Korea's law would see it

South Korea has a rule aimed at the same thing. Article 22-2 of its Network Act, the main law governing online services, requires apps to tell users clearly which device permissions are essential to the service and which are optional, and to get consent for each. Apps may not refuse service to someone who declines an optional permission.

The penalties are uneven. The Act's administrative fine of up to 30 million won (about $22,000) applies only when an app refuses service to someone who declined an optional permission, or when an operating-system maker, phone maker or similar supplier fails to give users a way to consent and withdraw. The Act sets no penalty for failing to obtain proper consent in the first place. The government can order the app to fix it, and ignoring that order carries the same 30 million won ceiling.

The bigger stick is Korea's Personal Information Protection Act. If the photos are treated as personal data collected without consent, the Personal Information Protection Commission can fine up to 3% of total revenue, excluding sales unrelated to the breach. An amendment passed in March this year lets it go up to 10% for intentional or grossly negligent breaches that affect 10 million people or more, or that repeat a violation within three years of an earlier fine. Those are ceilings; actual fines depend on the breach.

What you can check on your phone

The Italian order only covers users in Italy. But anyone can check how much of their gallery an app can see. On Android 14 and later, in apps built for Android 14 or newer, the photo permission prompt offers "Select photos and videos" as well as full access, so the app sees only the pictures you pick. Permissions you have already granted can be changed in your phone's app settings.

item.title: When a South Korean 'freelancer' is really an employee owed severance
item.description:
Who the law covers

South Korea's main employment law, the Labor Standards Act, and a separate law on severance pay protect employees, and only employees. So before anyone can claim severance pay, a paid weekly rest day or coverage under Korea's four social insurance schemes (pension, health, employment and workplace-injury insurance), there is a prior question: does the law see you as an employee at all?

The Labor Standards Act defines an employee as anyone who works for a business in return for wages, whatever the job. The title on the contract does not decide it. A deal labeled a freelance, service or commission agreement still creates an employee if the work looks like employment. The reverse can also hold: someone with an employment contract who in practice runs their own business may not be an employee.

The biggest sum riding on that answer is usually severance. Korea's Employee Retirement Benefit Security Act requires employers to pay it to anyone who has worked for at least a year, averaging at least 15 hours a week measured over four weeks. It applies to businesses of any size. The only exceptions are businesses that employ nobody but relatives living with the owner, and domestic workers hired by a household. Some other entitlements, such as annual paid leave and overtime premiums, depend on how many people a business employs.

This chapter reflects the Labor Standards Act as it stands from October 8, 2026, and the Employee Retirement Benefit Security Act as it stands from September 18, 2026.

How the rules changed

The test for who counts as an employee comes mostly from Supreme Court rulings rather than the text of the law, and it has shifted over time.

In a December 1994 ruling, the court said what matters is the reality of the work, not the form of the contract. But it asked whether the employer gave specific, individual instructions and supervision.

In December 2006, it spoke instead of substantial direction and supervision, a change widely read as lowering the bar. It also said courts should not easily deny employee status just because there was no fixed base pay, no income tax withheld from wages, or no enrollment in social insurance as an employee. Those, it reasoned, are things an employer can arrange as it likes.

From December 1, 2010, severance rules were extended to businesses with four or fewer employees, with at least half the normal amount owed for work up to the end of 2012 and the full amount from 2013.

In July 2024, it said that for people who find work through an app, judges should apply the same factors with the realities of platform work in mind, such as an algorithm deciding who gets which job.

So the common belief that a 3.3% tax deduction makes you a freelancer with no severance does not match the test courts have applied since 2006.

The problem: fake freelancers

Koreans call the practice "fake 3.3." A business hires people who work like employees but signs them up as self-employed contractors. Instead of withholding income tax from wages, it deducts a flat 3.3% (3% national tax on business income plus 0.3% local tax), the rate applied to payments to the self-employed. The business avoids social insurance contributions, severance and various allowances, and the worker loses all of them.

Using withholding-tax records from the National Tax Service and tips from labor groups, the Ministry of Employment and Labor, South Korea's labor department, picked 108 suspect workplaces and inspected them between December 1, 2025, and March 5, 2026. At 72 of them, or 67%, it found 1,070 employees signed up this way. Across all the workplaces inspected, 1,126 workers had been denied paid weekly rest days or annual leave, or had not received overtime, night or holiday pay, with unpaid wages totaling 685 million won, about $514,000.

The first case the ministry announced, in January 2026, was a popular restaurant business with six branches in Seoul that had registered 38 of its 52 workers, 73%, as self-employed. It owed 51 million won, about $38,000, to 65 current and former staff.

After the inspections ended, the ministry said on July 1 that all the workers found without coverage had been enrolled retroactively in employment and industrial accident insurance, and about 520 million won ($390,000) in unpaid premiums had been collected from the businesses.

Those were the cases inspectors found. Elsewhere, the burden falls on the worker: under current law, the person claiming to be an employee has to prove it. The contract and tax records say whatever the company wrote, so the worker has to show what the job was really like.

Where views differ

The first dispute is over what should count most. Korean courts put the weight on how far a company directs and supervises the work. Critics say they should look harder at how far a person depends on one company for a living. The argument has sharpened as platform work has grown, where an app gives the instructions and the jobs come from a single source.

The second is over who should carry the burden of proof. In January 2026, the labor ministry said it would introduce a presumption of employment: once someone shows they personally did work for another's business, they would be treated as an employee unless the business proves otherwise. The change would be made by amending the Labor Standards Act, and the ministry has said it aims to get it through the National Assembly by December 2026.

Supporters say the company, which holds the records, should carry the burden. One delivery rider, they point out, needed four and a half years from losing the job to being recognized in court as an employee. Opponents say a business would struggle to prove a negative, that there was no direction or supervision, so disputes would multiply, small firms would bear the cost and companies might hand out less work. As of November 15, 2026, the amendment had not passed.

What the courts decided

Korea's Supreme Court weighs a set of factors together. Does the company decide what the work is and supervise it substantially? Does it set the hours and the place? Can the worker use their own equipment or hire someone else to do the job? Do they carry the risk of profit and loss themselves? Is the pay a return for labor? And how long, and how exclusively, have they worked for the company?

The 2006 case involved instructors at a hagwon, a private cram school, preparing students for university entrance exams. Each year they signed what was called a lecture services contract. They were registered as businesses for tax purposes, had business income tax withheld and carried health insurance as individuals rather than through an employer. The court still found they were employees. The school set their arrival times, teaching hours and classrooms, and paid them an hourly rate multiplied by hours taught, so their pay did not change with the number of students.

The 2024 case involved a driver for Tada, an app-based service that rented out vans with a driver attached. The driver had signed a "freelance driver" contract with a staffing agency and was dropped from the roster by a group chat message. In this unfair-dismissal case, the court ruled that the driver was an employee, and that the employer was not the agency but Socar, the car-sharing company that supplied the vans and owned Tada's operator.

Courts also draw the line the other way. In the 1994 case, the plaintiffs were registered businesses that had taken on subcontracted construction work, each directing a crew of roughly 16 to 26 laborers they had hired themselves. The court found they were independent contractors, even though the company supplied equipment or materials, enrolled them in workplace-injury insurance and received daily reports from them.

Case law can change, and the spread of platform work could shift the test again.

Where that leaves us

Under today's test, neither the contract's label, nor the 3.3% deduction, nor the lack of social insurance settles that someone is not an employee. How tax was withheld is one factor among many. What matters is who decides the work, who fixes the hours and place, and whether the worker bears business risk with their own money.

Courts weigh the factors case by case, so people in the same line of work can get different answers. In a dispute, the evidence that shows the reality is ordinary: clock-in records, messages giving instructions, work rosters and records of pay received.

There are time limits too. Severance must be paid within 14 days of leaving, though both sides can agree to a later date if there is a special reason. Even so, interest of 20% a year runs from the day after that 14-day deadline. The 20% rate may not apply for any period in which it is reasonable for the employer to contest in court or before the Labor Relations Commission whether the money is owed at all, for instance whether the worker was an employee. The right to claim severance expires after three years.

Unpaid severance can be pursued through a complaint to a regional labor office or in court. Being recognized as an employee can also bring some tidying up. Income reported as business income may need to be corrected to wage income for tax purposes, and retroactive enrollment in social insurance can mean the worker owes their share of the premiums.

Do the math

Once someone is recognized as an employee, severance comes to roughly one month of average pay for each year worked. Years are counted as days worked divided by 365, so two years and two months earns about 2.17 years' worth.

Take someone paid 2.5 million won (about $1,880) a month with 3.3% withheld, who worked for two years (730 days) and left on September 30. Their severance would be about 4,891,304 won, roughly $3,670.

The calculation uses the 2.5 million won before the deduction, not the 2,417,500 won that reached the worker's account. The 3.3% is tax paid in advance; it does not reduce the wage. Try your own start date, last day of work and monthly pay in the calculator below.

If you run a business

A contract that says freelancer will not settle the matter if you direct the work and set the hours and the place. Korean courts look at how the work was actually done, not at the label on the contract.

If the worker is found to be an employee, unpaid severance and allowances and back premiums for social insurance can all come due at once. The labor ministry picks workplaces to inspect using withholding-tax records and anonymous tips.

Paying up does not end it. Failing to pay severance or wages within 14 days of someone leaving is a crime punishable by up to five years in prison or a fine of up to 50 million won, about $37,500. Prosecutors cannot proceed if the worker does not want the employer punished, but that exception does not apply while the employer is on the government's published list of wage defaulters.

Not handing over a written employment contract can bring a fine of up to 5 million won. Not issuing pay slips, or not registering a worker for employment insurance, can bring administrative penalties of up to 5 million won and 3 million won respectively.

Late severance can carry interest of 20% a year. And if wages were withheld deliberately, or left unpaid for three or more months in a year, the worker can ask a court for up to three times the amount owed.

item.title: What is opportunity cost? The real price of a college degree in South Korea
item.description:
Opportunity cost

Choosing one thing means giving up another. Economics starts there. Money and time are limited, so nobody gets everything.

The opportunity cost of a choice is the most valuable thing you gave up to make it. A movie ticket may cost 15,000 won, about $11, but the movie costs more than that. It also costs whatever else you could have done with those two hours.

So when economists say cost, they mean more than the money that left your wallet. The money you pay is part of it, because you could have spent it on something else. The real cost is what you paid plus what you gave up.

Tuition rises to 7.27 million won a year

On April 29, 2026, South Korea's Ministry of Education published its yearly tuition figures. Universities must report what they charge, and the ministry publishes the results. Across 192 four-year universities, average tuition for 2026 was 7,270,300 won a year, about $5,500. That was up 147,100 won, or 2.1%, from a year earlier.

Of the 192 schools, 130 raised tuition. Private universities averaged 8,231,500 won, about $6,200, and public ones 4,250,000 won, about $3,200.

That is where the news reports stopped: a year of college costs about 7.27 million won. Seen through opportunity cost, that figure is only part of the bill.

Adding up four years

Start with the money paid. Four years at average tuition come to 29.08 million won, about $21,800.

Then the money given up: the pay a student would have earned by working instead. Assume full-time work for all 48 months, paid at the lowest legal rate, the minimum wage. In 2026 it is 10,320 won an hour, about $7.75. For a full-time, 40-hour week the government puts that at 2,156,880 won a month, about $1,620. The figure includes a paid weekly rest day that Korean law requires. Over 48 months that is 103.53 million won, about $77,700.

Together they make 132.61 million won, close to $100,000. Tuition is 22% of that. The other 78% never appears on a bill. Most of the cost of a degree is not tuition. It is the pay that could have been earned in those years.

What counts and what doesn't

What about food and rent? People eat and need a place to sleep whether or not they study. Money you would spend either way is not given up, so it is not part of the opportunity cost. If college means moving out and renting a room, only the extra spending counts.

A scholarship lowers the money paid. A part-time job during the term lowers the pay given up. So does any stretch the student would have spent looking for work instead of working. For someone who could earn well above the minimum wage, the pay given up is larger.

That is why opportunity cost differs from person to person. Two students at the same school paying the same tuition can face very different costs.

Why people still go

A high cost does not make a choice wrong. It is worth it when the gain is larger.

The OECD's yearly report, Education at a Glance, was released in September 2026. It found that among Korean adults aged 25 to 64, university graduates earned 31.8% more than high school graduates in 2024. The average across OECD countries was 39.3%, so the reward for a degree in Korea is below the rich-country average.

Here is a rough calculation. Suppose a high school graduate earns the minimum wage. A university graduate would then earn about 686,000 won more each month, about $515. Covering 132.61 million won with that gap would take 193 months, or about 16 years.

Set that against a working life of several decades, and read it with care. It applies a gap measured across all working ages to someone just starting out. It ignores taxes and pay rises, and it treats a won earned 16 years from now as equal to a won today. It also compares averages, and the gap varies widely by field and employer. And it leaves out things that are hard to price, such as how easy it is to find work and what kind of work it is. Still, it shows one thing. Whether to go to college is not only a question about tuition. It is a question about what you give up and what you get.

Same question, different answers

Think of an athlete who can join a professional team straight out of high school. Going to college would cost several playing years and the salary that comes with them. The opportunity cost is very high, so many put college off.

Most South Koreans make the other choice. In 2025, 71.1% of Koreans aged 25 to 34 had finished a two-year college or university degree, the highest share in the OECD.

Neither choice is the right one for everyone. The calculation is the same, but the numbers that go into it are not.

Using it when you read the news

Opportunity cost applies beyond personal choices. A company that builds a factory gives up the other investments that money could have funded. A government that spends in one place has less to spend elsewhere.

So when a headline says something costs a certain amount, ask one more question. What else could that money and time have been used for?

item.title: Korea suspends its 140% margin-loan rule. A 130% line delays margin calls less than it sounds
item.description:
Ten points lower, five points more

Say you put in 10 million won (about $7,480) of your own money, borrow another 10 million won from your broker and buy 20 million won of shares. If the broker's line is 140%, a 30% fall in the shares triggers a forced sale. At 130%, the trigger moves to a 35% fall.

So a 10-point cut in the line buys 5 points of room. If you had borrowed only 5 million won, the extra room shrinks to 3.3 points.

That is the arithmetic behind the main step Korea has taken against forced selling in this month's slide.

What Korea suspended

In Korea, brokers lend directly to clients who want to buy shares on margin. Under the Financial Investment Services regulations, Article 4-25(3), a broker must hold collateral worth at least 140% of the loan when it lends, and then keep the account at the ratio set by its own internal rules. When an account falls below that line and the client does not top it up, the broker sells the shares, typically within a day or two.

On November 6, after the KOSPI fell sharply following the US midterm elections, the government held an emergency market meeting. The Financial Services Commission said the collateral requirement would be waived for three months from November 9, to stop a wave of forced sales from pushing prices down further. The waiver comes as a no-action letter from the Financial Supervisory Service: regulators will not penalize brokers that let accounts fall below 140%. Each broker decides what to do with that freedom.

Korean media reported that some large brokers cut their line for domestic shares to 130%, while others let clients in roughly the 130% to 140% band apply to delay a forced sale by a day; some allow it only once, others ask clients to reapply daily, and at least one limited its cut to one month. They reported that the waiver runs until January 31.

How to find your own line

The collateral ratio is the value of the shares in the account divided by the loan. In the example above it starts at 200%: 20 million won of shares against 10 million won borrowed. At 14 million won of shares it is 140%, and at 13 million won it is 130%.

As a formula, the fall that triggers a sale is 1 minus (the line × the loan ÷ the amount you first bought). The more you borrow, the less room you have, but the more a lower line helps. You can try your own numbers in the calculator below.

Brokers count slightly differently. Some include cash and other shares as collateral, and some add accrued interest to the loan. The ratio shown in your brokerage app is the one that matters.

The 'forced selling surge' is a different number

Korean investors can be forced to sell in two ways. One is a margin loan that runs short of collateral. The other is an unpaid purchase: Korean brokers let clients buy shares before paying in full, with settlement two business days later. If the cash is not there by then, the broker sells. The waiver covers only margin loans.

Some of the figures reported as a jump in forced selling in the first week are for unpaid purchases. On November 9, the day the waiver began, those sales reached 37.9 billion won (about $28 million), more than five times the previous trading day, according to Korean media. The waiver does not apply to those, so the number alone says little about whether it worked.

Last time, three months became six

Korea has done this before. On July 1, 2022, with the KOSPI dipping below 2,300 during the day as interest rates rose, the commission waived the same requirement from July 4 to September 30. On September 23 it extended the waiver by three months to the end of the year.

This year's announcement says nothing about an extension. The 2022 announcement said the waiver could be extended if needed, and it was, once.

A delayed sale is not a cancelled one

A lower line or a one-day delay does not shrink the debt. Interest keeps running, and if prices keep falling the shares may be sold later at a lower price, deepening the loss. If prices recover, the sale is avoided.

Brokers carry risk too. If a forced sale does not cover the loan, the broker absorbs the shortfall. Korean media reported that this is why some brokers chose case-by-case delays over a blanket cut.

For anyone holding shares bought on margin, three checks matter: whether your broker lowered its line automatically or requires an application, what your current ratio is, and whether adding cash or repaying part of the loan would lift it. The date to watch is January 31, when the waiver is reported to end. If brokers go back to 140%, accounts sitting between 130% and 140% will need more collateral by then.

item.title: Officials blame an overloaded router for the four-hour US ground stop. Canceled flights mean full refunds
item.description:
A rare order to stop every takeoff

The FAA ordered a nationwide ground stop around 4 p.m. Eastern on Friday, November 13. A ground stop keeps new flights on the ground; it does not shut the airspace.

The order was lifted at 8:15 p.m. Eastern, just over four hours later. Cancellations and delays spilled into the weekend as airlines moved planes and crews back into place.

Why one communications failure stops the whole country

The FAA said communication problems were affecting multiple Air Route Traffic Control Centers. Unlike airport towers, which handle takeoffs and landings, these regional centers guide planes once they climb away from the airport and cruise at high altitude. Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said the issue affected all of the centers and blamed aging air traffic control equipment.

Controllers talk to pilots by radio, assigning altitudes and routes. If that link is unreliable, the safe move is to stop adding planes to the sky. That is why departures stop first while flights already in the air are handled case by case.

Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin said the outage did not appear to be a cyberattack and seemed "mechanically driven." Questions also turned to SMART, an AI traffic-management tool the FAA expanded to all centers three days earlier. Its developer, Air Space Intelligence, said the ground stop was not caused by SMART. Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy later said there was "no possible way" SMART could have caused it.

9/11, 2023 and now

Nationwide ground stops are extremely rare; this was only the second since the September 11 attacks. According to the 9/11 Commission Report, the first hijacked jet hit the World Trade Center's North Tower at 8:46 a.m. and the second hit the South Tower at 9:03. The FAA's Command Center ordered a nationwide ground stop 22 minutes later, at 9:25. After a third plane struck the Pentagon at 9:37, it went further at 9:42 and ordered every aircraft already in the air to land at the nearest airport.

The most recent was on January 11, 2023, when the system that sends safety notices to pilots failed. The FAA's preliminary review found that contract personnel had unintentionally deleted files while syncing the main database with its backup.

This time, officials say it was equipment, not an attack. The next day Duffy said L3Harris, a longtime FAA contractor, had upgraded copper wire to fiber-optic cable at a remote site during routine maintenance, and a router then overloaded a critical communications system. Whether the fault lies with the work or the equipment is still under investigation.

If your flight was canceled, you get your money back

Under Department of Transportation rules, a canceled flight is any flight that was in the airline's reservation system when you bought the ticket and did not operate. The reason does not matter, whether weather, air traffic control or a mechanical problem. If you turn down the rebooking or a voucher, the airline owes you a full refund, taxes and fees included, to your original form of payment.

Big schedule changes count too: a departure moved three or more hours earlier (six for international trips), an arrival three or more hours later (six for international), a different airport, or more connections. Airlines can only give you a voucher if you agree to it.

Refunds are due within seven business days for credit card purchases and 20 calendar days for other payment methods, counted from when the refund becomes due. Airlines have had to issue these refunds automatically since October 28, 2024.

Who pays for the refunds

The airlines do, even though this outage was not their fault. There is no federal program that reimburses carriers for losses caused by an air traffic control failure. A refund is not compensation; it is the fare for a flight the airline did not fly.

Meals and hotels are another matter. The Transportation Department's customer service dashboard lists what each airline promises when a cancellation or delay is within its control, such as maintenance or crew shortages. Weather and air traffic control problems are not, so airlines are not required to cover meals or hotel rooms. Travelers stranded overnight by this ground stop may have to pay for their own rooms.

Foreign airlines are covered too

The rules apply to any airline flying to, from or within the United States, so Korean Air and Asiana passengers on US routes have the same right to a refund as travelers on American carriers.

If you were connecting through a US airport, check every leg of the trip before accepting a new itinerary.

item.title: Trump picks talks over robotics tariffs under Section 232. Autos took that path in 2019 and got a 25% tariff
item.description:
Talks, not tariffs, for now

President Donald Trump has found that imports of robots, industrial machinery and their parts threaten to impair US national security. But his October 28 proclamation, issued under Section 232 of the Trade Expansion Act of 1962, stops short of tariffs. Section 232 lets the president restrict imports on national security grounds; it is the law behind the steel, aluminum and auto tariffs.

Instead, it tells the commerce secretary and the US trade representative to negotiate with whichever trading partners they see fit, and to report on progress within 180 days. A progress report is due by April 26, 2027. No country is named.

What the Commerce Department found

The proclamation summarizes the department's findings. Robots and industrial machinery are used to build missiles, aircraft and ships, and products made with them reach all 16 of the sectors the US designates as critical infrastructure. It says the machines supported about $7.1 trillion in US manufacturing shipments in 2024, and about $86 billion worth of equipment produced that year.

The US relies on imports for most types of robots and industrial machinery, the proclamation says, and the value of those imports has grown over the past decade. It also flags cybersecurity risks from robots made by "certain foreign entities", because the machines handle sensitive data. It does not say which countries it means.

The autos precedent

Trump has tried talks-first before. It ended in tariffs. On May 17, 2019, during his first term, Trump found that imported cars and auto parts threatened national security and directed the trade representative to negotiate with the European Union, Japan and others.

His March 26, 2025 proclamation records what happened next: the negotiations "did not lead to any agreements" of the kind Section 232 contemplates. Commerce told him the security concerns "remain and have escalated" since its February 2019 report, and he imposed a 25% tariff on imported cars and auto parts. The gap between ordering talks and imposing tariffs was nearly six years.

South Korean cars were hit by that tariff too. Under a trade deal Seoul later struck with Washington, Korean cars entering the US from November 1, 2025 face a combined rate of 15%, including the standard US import duty.

Four times this year

The talks-first approach has become a pattern in 2026. Proclamations on processed critical minerals (January 14), commercial aircraft and jet engines (July 9), wind turbines (October 22) and now robotics all found a security threat and ordered negotiations rather than new tariffs. Some wind turbine parts already pay Section 232 tariffs on steel, aluminum and copper.

The critical minerals deadline passed on July 13. As of November 14, HOLT found no follow-up proclamation in the Federal Register imposing tariffs on those minerals. A missed deadline does not trigger tariffs automatically, and the autos case shows the threat can resurface years later.

What can happen after 180 days

If no agreement is reached within 180 days, or one is not carried out or proves ineffective, the statute says the president "shall" take whatever other action he deems necessary. What that action is remains his call. The robotics proclamation lists the options: tariffs, duties, quotas, fees, or a program to reward new investment in US production of robots and machinery.

None of that has been decided. The commerce secretary will keep monitoring imports and is to flag any need for further action. For manufacturers in South Korea, Japan and Europe that sell machinery to the US, the dates to watch are the progress report due in late April 2027 and any tariff proclamation that follows.

item.title: After a near 24-hour Microsoft 365 outage, businesses can claim 25% or 50% credits. Home users can't
item.description:
What went down, and why

The outage began at 11:20 a.m. Eastern on Thursday, November 12, and services were only broadly restored nearly 24 hours later. Outlook, Teams and Copilot failed for users around the world, from government offices to hospitals. South Korean companies also reported work grinding to a halt.

Microsoft first blamed an earlier network capacity upgrade. Its preliminary post-incident report on November 16 traced the outage instead to a latent bug in a fix rolled out to its networking gateway servers in July, which surfaced when Teams traffic was shifted onto the same gateways and about 14% of their capacity was already offline for an unrelated reason. The company said the outage was not related to a cyberattack or to AI agents. "We are deeply sorry for the disruption this incident has caused our customers and partners," the company said.

For businesses, the next question is money. Microsoft's answer is written in its service-level agreement, and it measures downtime in a way that is easy to miss.

Downtime is counted in user-minutes

Picture a power company that pays each household for the hours it actually spent in the dark, not for how long the blackout lasted somewhere in the city. Microsoft counts downtime the same way, in what it calls user-minutes.

Under the SLA, downtime for Exchange Online, Microsoft's business email service, means any time users cannot send or receive email through Outlook on the web. For Teams, it means users cannot send instant messages or start online meetings. Each incident's minutes are multiplied by the number of users affected, added up across the month, and compared with the month's total user-minutes.

If uptime falls below 99.9%, the credit is 25% of that month's fee for the service. Below 99%, it is 50%. Below 95%, it is 100%. November has 30 days, or 43,200 minutes. If every user is hit, that works out to more than 43.2 minutes of downtime for 25%, more than 7 hours 12 minutes for 50%, and more than 36 hours for 100%.

Does a 24-hour outage mean 50%?

Only if enough of your staff were cut off. If every user lost email for the full 24 hours, uptime for the month would be about 96.7%, which is in the 50% tier. In practice, outages hit people unevenly. What counts is the total of users multiplied by minutes. Put in terms of people cut off for the full 24 hours, more than 30% of users gets you to 50%, more than 3% gets you 25%, and 3% or less gets nothing. Half your staff losing email for 15 hours each also lands in the 50% tier.

This outage alone cannot reach the 100% tier. If another incident hits the same service in the same month, its user-minutes are added in.

A credit is not a cash refund. It comes off a future bill, and only for the service that failed; some small-volume licensing plans extend the subscription by extra days instead. Microsoft makes the final call on each claim, an alert on the status page does not guarantee a credit, and time when Outlook on the web still worked, or was merely slow, does not count as downtime. If your company pays for a bundle, the credit is worked out only for the parts that failed, not for the whole plan.

Personal and free accounts

The SLA is part of Microsoft's volume licensing agreements for organizations. It says free services and previews are not eligible for credits.

Microsoft 365 Personal and Family plans and free Outlook.com accounts fall under the Microsoft Services Agreement instead, which makes no uptime promise and states that all online services suffer occasional disruptions. Under the US version, if you do have a claim, you can recover only direct damages, capped at your fee for the month the problem happened, or $10 if the service is free. The terms vary by country: the Korean version, governed by Korean law, makes Microsoft liable for damage caused by its intent or negligence, though not for unusual losses such as lost business unless it acted intentionally or with gross negligence. Outside such cases, Microsoft says it is not liable for disruption or loss caused by outages.

Lost business is on you

The business SLA calls service credits the "sole and exclusive remedy" for performance or availability problems. A missed deal or a delayed contract is not covered, and customers cannot simply withhold part of their bill.

In other words, the most a company can expect from this outage is half of one month's fee for each affected service.

How to claim, and by when

Credits are not automatic. For services other than Azure, claims sent to Microsoft are due by the end of the month after the incident, so November's outage must be claimed by December 31. Partners work on their own billing month, so their cutoff can differ; tell them early. Microsoft says it typically processes claims within 45 days.

Companies that buy directly from Microsoft file a claim with Microsoft support. Many others buy through Cloud Solution Provider (CSP) partners. In that case the partner files the claim, and resellers that buy from those partners cannot file it themselves.

Gather the outage incident ID from the Service health page in the Microsoft 365 admin center, your tenant ID (the unique number for your organization's Microsoft 365 account), the time and duration of the downtime, and the number and locations of affected users. If a partner is filing for you, it also needs an email from you asking for the credit, sent from your company's domain; Microsoft does not accept personal addresses as evidence.

item.title: California voters reject Prop 40 billionaire tax, likely keep tax on high earners
item.description:
Three tax questions, three different answers

California voters on November 3 split on three ballot measures about taxing the rich. With counting still being finalized, Secretary of State figures as of the afternoon of November 12 show Proposition 40, a one-time 5% tax on the net worth of billionaires, failing by 52.4% to 47.6%.

Proposition 3, which makes a 2012 income tax increase on high earners permanent, is passing comfortably, with 60.7% of the vote. Proposition 42, a constitutional amendment that would bar new state taxes on owning stocks and other personal property, leads 51.4% to 48.6%, a margin of about 330,000 votes. None of the results is certified yet, and Proposition 42's lead is the only one close enough to matter.

What the billionaire tax would have done

Proposition 40 would have applied to billionaires who were California residents on January 1, 2026, ten months before the vote. They would have owed 5% of their net worth, due in 2027, with the option to spread payments over five years at extra cost. Real estate, pensions and retirement accounts were generally excluded. A billionaire with $10 billion in taxable net worth would have owed $500 million.

The Legislative Analyst's Office, the legislature's nonpartisan fiscal adviser, estimated the tax would raise tens of billions of dollars over several years, with 90% earmarked for health care. It also warned that some billionaires might leave the state, which could cost California less than $1 billion a year in income tax. A few hundred people with a net worth above $1 billion live in California, according to the office.

The tax on the rich that voters kept

Proposition 3 extends rates first approved by voters in 2012 under Proposition 30 and extended through 2030 by Proposition 55 in 2016. The higher rates apply only to the top 2% of taxpayers, who pay about half of all state income tax. The analyst's office expects the measure to keep $5 billion to $15 billion a year flowing to the state, depending largely on the stock market. Roughly 40% will go to schools and community colleges.

One difference is between taxing what people earn and taxing what they own. Another is that Proposition 3 continued an existing tax, while Proposition 40 would have created a new one. An income tax is paid out of money that came in that year. A wealth tax is due whether or not the assets produced any cash, which can force owners of stock-heavy fortunes to sell shares to pay it.

A constitutional lock on wealth taxes

California already taxes some personal property, such as vehicles through the annual license fee and business equipment through county property taxes. It does not tax simply owning financial assets like stocks or investment accounts. Proposition 42 would make it unconstitutional for the state to start.

The measure also limits retroactive taxes, which the analyst's office illustrates with a tax on money earned two years earlier. Proposition 40's residency date, January 1, 2026, fell ten months before Election Day. A related measure, Proposition 41, which would have added audits of new special taxes and made it harder to keep their revenue outside the state spending limit, failed with 55.1% voting no. The analyst's office had warned that if Proposition 41 drew more yes votes than Proposition 40, courts could block Proposition 40 even if a majority backed it. Both measures failed, so the conflict never arose.

Wealth taxes elsewhere

Annual net wealth taxes have been retreating for decades. According to a 2018 OECD study, the number of member countries that levied one on individuals fell from 12 in 1990 to four in 2017: France, Norway, Spain and Switzerland. The OECD said repeals were usually justified on efficiency and administrative grounds, and that with a few exceptions the taxes raised very little money.

South Korea, where this publication is based, also does not tax simply holding shares or bank deposits. Its taxes on ownership fall mainly on real estate, through a local property tax paid by all owners and a national comprehensive real estate holding tax on owners of high-value property, and also on some movable property such as cars and ships.

What happens next

Results become final once counties finish counting and the Secretary of State certifies them. Every precinct has reported, but ballots remain to be counted. If Proposition 42 holds its lead, a similar wealth tax could return only as a constitutional amendment that also overrides the new provision. Supporters of Proposition 40 have been reported as saying they will try again. The analyst's office said Proposition 42 could mean state revenue grows more slowly in the future, without estimating by how much or when.

item.title: The US moves to seize $1.2bn from North Korea's Binance hack. Getting it back is another matter
item.description:
A familiar face on a video call

A contact you know from Telegram asks to catch up on Zoom and sends a link. You click it, and there they are on screen. Then they message you: nobody can hear you, so click this link to fix your audio. That is how a North Korean hacking scheme the FBI calls FaceStealer works, according to an alert the bureau issued on November 12.

The face on screen is a video of an earlier victim, recorded in secret. The meeting page is a fake copy of Zoom or Teams run by the hackers, and the "fix" link installs malware. The hackers take whatever crypto they can reach, then use the new victim's contacts and webcam footage to go after the next person. The FBI says the scheme has netted more than $400 million in crypto over the past 18 months. Agents seized more than 900 webcam videos of victims.

The same day, the Justice Department said it had seized cloud-based infrastructure used in the scheme. It also announced a separate case. Around October 29, North Korean military hackers stole more than $6 billion from Binance, one of the world's biggest crypto exchanges, in a theft the department says was separate from FaceStealer. Prosecutors have won court approval to seize or restrain more than $1.2 billion of it.

Seized is not the same as returned

The announcement covers three different stages. The first is a freeze: an exchange or a token issuer blocks a wallet so the coins cannot move. US agencies and private companies have together frozen more than $2.7 billion, less than half of what was taken.

The second is seizure or restraint, which takes a court order. That is the $1.2 billion. The third is forfeiture: the government has to prove in court that the money came from crime. Victims and other claimants can ask for the money back as part of that process.

The hackers are still moving the rest. The department says the group, which the FBI calls TraderTraitor, keeps laundering the coins. It uses bridges, which move coins from one blockchain to another, mixers, which blend them with other people's coins, and exchanges. Tracing, freezing, seizing and forfeiture efforts continue, the department says.

What happened to Bitfinex's bitcoin

The closest precedent is the 2016 Bitfinex hack. In August of that year, about 119,754 bitcoin were stolen from the exchange. The government seized the hacker's wallet on January 31, 2022, nearly five and a half years later. By then about 25,000 coins had been laundered away; 94,643 were still in the wallet.

Seizure did not end it. In October 2024, prosecutors asked the court to hand back that bitcoin, plus coins later split off from it, to Bitfinex in kind, as coins rather than cash. They valued the lot at more than $6 billion. A month later, Bitfinex told the judge in a letter that it had been trying to recover the coins for nearly nine years. It had covered all customer losses with its own money by April 3, 2017, about eight months after the hack, so it argued that it alone had taken the loss.

In January 2025, prosecutors added a legal wrinkle. Because the defendants pleaded guilty to money laundering, not to the hack itself, Bitfinex was not a "victim" of those crimes under the federal law that makes restitution mandatory, they wrote. They argued the coins could still go back because the defendants agreed to that in their plea deals. Prosecutors said other seized assets should go through a separate forfeiture proceeding, where third parties can file claims.

Who would get Binance's money?
