Binance has said it will cover customers' losses with its own funds, according to multiple reports. The Justice Department has not said who would receive any coins it eventually recovers, or how.

The setup could look similar: an exchange that has promised to absorb its customers' losses, then claims whatever is recovered. The Bitfinex route, though, is not open here. In that case, the hacker was arrested in the US and pleaded guilty, and returning the coins was written into the plea deals. North Korean military hackers are unlikely to face a US courtroom. The Justice Department has not said which process it will use. One option that needs no defendant is civil forfeiture: a lawsuit the government brings against the property itself.

How to spot a fake meeting

The FBI says the hackers go after people in crypto and web3, and increasingly after open-source software maintainers, whose accounts could let them slip malicious code into widely used software. Invitations arrive from hijacked or newly created Telegram, LinkedIn, Slack and Discord accounts.

The bureau's advice: join calls from the official Zoom or Teams app with a meeting code, not from a link. Keep your camera off until you can see and talk to the person who invited you. Never run a script or paste a command to "update" a meeting app. Confirm the meeting through a different channel, such as a phone call or text.

If you think you have been hit, move your crypto to a new wallet created on a device that never touched the conversation. The FBI says the hackers have copied recovery phrases and waited months, sometimes more than a year, for balances to grow before emptying them.

item.title: Trinidad and Tobago's buggery law breaches rights, Privy Council rules
item.description:
The ruling

Five judges of the Judicial Committee of the Privy Council ruled unanimously on November 10 that two sections of Trinidad and Tobago's Sexual Offences Act 1986 breach the right to respect for private and family life in the country's constitution.

Trinidad and Tobago, a Caribbean nation off the coast of Venezuela, became independent from Britain in 1962 but still sends its final appeals to the Privy Council in London, a court staffed mainly by UK Supreme Court justices.

What the law punishes

Section 13 makes buggery a crime whether or not both people consent. Since a 2012 amendment, the maximum sentence has been 25 years. Section 16 criminalises "serious indecency", with exceptions only for husband and wife, or a man and a woman aged 16 or over who both consent, acting in private.

The case was brought in February 2017 by Jason Jones, a gay man born in 1964 and raised in Port of Spain, the capital. He asked the courts to declare that the two sections breached his constitutional rights. No one had been prosecuted under them for many years, but he said their existence alone harmed him. In unchallenged evidence he described near-daily harassment and abuse in public, avoiding public transport for fear of his safety, and being attacked several times with rocks, glass bottles and pieces of wood at his performances as a singer, without protection from the police. He lived in constant fear of arrest and punishment. After years of harassment and discrimination he moved to England in 1996, returning to live in Trinidad from 2010 to 2014.

The trial judge agreed that the law made his private life criminal, ignored his dignity to choose whom to love and live with, treated him differently from heterosexual citizens and gave others a reason to see him as of lesser value.

Two shields, both rejected

The government argued that the constitution protected the law in two ways. The first was a "savings clause". Section 6 shields laws that existed before the 1976 constitution from rights challenges. Section 6(2) covers later laws that re-enact those old laws with changes: where a new law restricts rights further than the old one, the old rules snap back in its place. Sex between men was already a crime under a 1925 colonial-era ordinance.

In March 2025 the Court of Appeal accepted the savings-clause argument and put the older rules back in place. Under that ruling, sex between consenting adult men would still have been a crime, with a maximum of five years. The Privy Council did not. The 1986 act said it would "repeal and replace" the old law, the judges noted, and it was a fresh, comprehensive code drafted after a Law Commission review. Clauses that shield old laws from rights challenges should be read narrowly, they said, or they would hollow out the constitution's purpose.

The second shield was section 13. A law that declares it overrides fundamental rights and is passed by three-fifths of all members of each house stands even if it conflicts with those rights, unless it is shown not to be "reasonably justifiable" in a society that respects individual rights. The 1986 act was passed that way.

Judged by today's standards

Every judge in the lower courts had found the law unjustifiable under section 13. Only at the Privy Council did the government argue that justification should be measured by the standards of 1986, since attitudes had shifted over 40 years. The court disagreed: the test applies when a person's rights are before the court, which is now.

The government's only justification was that the law was traditional. The judges said the mere survival of a repressive colonial-era law could not be a legitimate aim, and a living social tradition could count only with evidence that it is still widely accepted. The government had offered none. Even if tradition were a legitimate aim, they said, the law intrudes too deeply into private life to strike a fair balance.

What's next

The core ruling is settled; only the exact wording of the fix is not. The Privy Council will take further written arguments before issuing a final order.

The ruling already says the two sections cannot be used against private, consensual sex between adults of the same sex. Its provisional view is to keep the fix ordered by the High Court on September 20, 2018, which limits section 13 to sex without consent and cuts the maximum sentence to five years. Lawyers for Mr Jones want both sections struck out entirely, arguing that other criminal laws already cover any conduct that should be punished; the judges said tidying up overlapping offences is a job for Parliament, not the courts.

The section 6(2) part of the ruling is unlikely to matter elsewhere. The judges called section 6(2) apparently unique: neither side's lawyers could point to a similar clause anywhere else. But the court's other points, that clauses shielding old laws must be read narrowly and that justification is judged by today's standards, could be cited in challenges elsewhere. Advocacy groups from Belize and Bermuda were among those who intervened in the case.

item.title: The SS United States is becoming a reef, and the paint left on board is the fight
item.description:
From a Philadelphia pier to the Gulf floor

Okaloosa County, Florida, began sinking the SS United States on the afternoon of November 11, about 22 nautical miles southwest of Destin. If all goes to plan, the ship will rest in about 180 feet of water with its upper deck 55 to 60 feet below the surface.

The 990-foot liner set the transatlantic speed record for an ocean liner on its maiden voyage in 1952, a record no liner has beaten. Retired in 1969, it passed through several owners and spent its last nearly 30 years tied up at a pier in Philadelphia.

The county says a full restoration would have cost hundreds of millions of dollars, leaving a choice between scrap and a reef. It is betting on fish and tourists: a wreck this size should draw reef fish such as snapper and grouper, as well as open-water hunters such as tuna and mackerel that gather around large structures to feed on the smaller fish they attract, and with them divers, charter fishing boats and commercial fishermen. It has budgeted $13 million for the whole project: buying the ship, towing it, cleaning it and helping fund a museum on land. The money comes from a tourist tax on short-term rentals and from local partners, not the county's general fund.

The federal cleaning checklist

The county says it prepared the ship under a 2006 guide from the Environmental Protection Agency and the Maritime Administration, the national standard for readying vessels to become reefs.

The guide asks for fuel and oil to be removed so no sheen appears when the ship sinks, and for loose asbestos to be removed, with crumbling asbestos removed or sealed. It says every manufactured item containing 50 parts per million or more of solid PCBs should come out, along with all liquid PCBs. PCBs, industrial chemicals once common in ship wiring and paint, have been banned from US production since 1979.

The paint rules are looser. Peeling paint should go, the guide says, as should active anti-fouling coatings on the hull. The guide notes that old marine paint can contain heavy metals such as lead, chromium and zinc, but intact paint, it says, generally does not need to be removed.

The guide also says it is not a regulation and binds no agency. Sinking a ship still needs separate approvals, such as a permit from the Army Corps of Engineers.

The carrier that went down with its PCBs

One big ship prepared under that guide, then still a draft, was the aircraft carrier Oriskany, 911 feet long, sunk about 23 miles south of Pensacola.

On February 15, 2006, the EPA gave the Navy and the State of Florida a risk-based approval to sink it with an estimated 700 pounds of PCBs still in gaskets, cables, insulation and heat-resistant paint, after a risk assessment found no unreasonable risk. The approval came with a condition: Florida's Fish and Wildlife Conservation Commission had to monitor whether fish caught at the site stayed safe to eat.

The EPA guide puts the Oriskany project's cost at $15.63 million, including $3.74 million for PCB modeling and risk assessment. The SS United States took a different route. The county says its wiring, fuel and non-metal fittings were stripped out during about a year of work in Mobile, Alabama, and that all required cleanup is complete.

This time, the fight is over paint

Preservationists and some environmental campaigners have targeted the zinc chromate primer on the ship's steel. They argue that as it breaks down it will release hexavalent chromium, a known carcinogen, into the Gulf and its fish. A preservation group asked a court to halt the sinking and lost.

The county counters that the coating is not a federally regulated substance when it comes to artificial reefs, and that the saltwater Gulf is nothing like a drinking-water supply.

The guide cannot settle the argument. It flags chromium as a possible paint ingredient, yet, for paint, sets a removal threshold only for PCBs and lets intact paint stay. The county has published no figure for how much chromium remains on board.

What comes next

The ship went down far more slowly than planned. Officials had said it could sink in under an hour once flooded; instead the work dragged on through the afternoon and into the evening, according to news reports. As of late November 11, US Eastern time, the county had not announced that the ship had settled on the bottom.

The next question is what the wreck releases. The county has not said whether fish at the site will be tested, as they were required to be at the Oriskany. The county plans to open the wreck to divers and fishing boats once it settles.

item.title: South Korea moves to stop apps hiding the 'delete account' button
item.description:
Two screens, no further

South Korea's Fair Trade Commission, the country's competition and consumer watchdog, has proposed that online businesses be treated as possibly breaching e-commerce law if they hide the button for deleting an account. The draft change to its consumer protection guideline for online commerce, announced on November 10, is open for comment until November 26, under a notice period that began on November 6, and is not yet final. The guideline does not create new law; it sets out how the commission reads the existing e-commerce act and gives examples of conduct that may break it.

The test is how far a user has to dig. If a site puts its sign-up button on the home page, the delete-account button must appear either on the first screen a user sees after logging in or on a screen that page links to directly. It does not matter whether that second screen is called 'My page' or 'Manage account.'

Being on the second screen is not enough on its own. The draft also lists burying the button under menus where users would not expect it, such as profile editing, security settings or subscription management, as an example of a possible breach.

Extra hoops at the exit

The draft names two more tactics. One is demanding phone, automated-call or email verification to delete an account, cancel an order or end a contract when the check is not essential to that step and was not required at sign-up or purchase.

The other is forcing users to answer a survey about why they are leaving before they can go on. Both are listed as examples of obstructing cancellation.

The draft also covers returns. Korean law lets sellers refuse to take back made-to-order goods only when a return would cause them serious harm they cannot recover from. Telling shoppers that an item cannot be returned simply because it was made to order, with notices such as 'produced after you order, no returns,' would be listed as an example of a breach.

A separate recommendation, not a rule, asks sites not to make users scroll a long way to find the seller's address, phone number and business registration number.

From advice to a draft example of a breach

Korea already bans making it hard to cancel. Since February 14, 2025, its e-commerce law has outlawed six kinds of manipulative design, often called dark patterns, including hidden renewals and making it harder to cancel than to sign up.

Guidance on how to read that law took effect on October 24, 2025. Asking users to confirm or reconsider their decision unnecessarily, two or more times, became an example of a breach. Button placement did not. Advice to put the button in an account menu appeared only among the guideline's recommendations, which businesses are asked, not required, to follow.

The new draft moves button placement into the part of the guideline that sets out what breaks the law. The commission says it is targeting the issues that produced the most violations and complaints.

The draft does not cite them, but checks from February to July 2025 show the backdrop. The commission and the Korea Consumer Agency got 36 companies to fix, or submit plans to fix, 45 suspected dark patterns. Obstructing cancellation was the most common type, with 15 cases. Nine were at rental and car-rental firms, some of which had accepted cancellations only by phone and now allow them online. Those cases involved phone-only cancellation and repeated 'are you sure?' steps, not button placement.

How Germany and the US compare

Germany went further in July 2022. Section 312k of its civil code requires a cancellation button for paid subscriptions and other ongoing contracts that can be signed online.

The button may carry only the words 'cancel contracts here' or something equally clear. It must lead straight to a confirmation page with a 'cancel now' button, and both must be available at all times and easy to reach. Financial services are exempt.

In the United States, the Federal Trade Commission voted 3-2 in October 2024 for a rule requiring cancellation to be at least as easy as signing up. On July 8, 2025, the Eighth Circuit Court of Appeals struck the rule down in full.

The court ruled on procedure, not substance. Once an FTC administrative law judge found the rule would cost the economy more than $100 million a year, the agency was required to publish a preliminary regulatory analysis, and it did not.

Korea's draft does not dictate button wording or a confirmation step, as Germany's law does. Instead it sets a maximum depth. The US rule created new duties; Korea's draft only sets out how the regulator reads a ban already in statute.

What happens next

Comments can be sent to the commission's consumer transactions policy division by post, email or fax until November 26. The commission will also consult other ministries before finalising the change. No start date has been set.

The examples describe conduct that may break the law; each case is still judged on its facts. After its 2025 checks, the commission said firms that failed to carry out promised fixes would face corrective orders and fines.

If the draft is adopted, services that tuck the delete button deep inside their settings will have to redesign.

item.title: Everyone flying to the US must now sign an Ebola form, as the earlier entry ban lapses
item.description:
A form for everyone on board

Since 11:59 p.m. Eastern time on November 3, no one can board a US-bound flight from abroad without signing a short form. It says the traveler has not been in the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC) in the past 21 days. The assistant secretary for health at the Department of Health and Human Services signed the order on October 22. The CDC enforces it. It applies to everyone, including US citizens and green card holders: an American who was in Congo in the past 21 days cannot board without a CDC exemption.

An amended order on October 28 extended the rule to crew members and spelled out that cargo flights count. Passengers who are only connecting through the United States were covered from the start. The order runs through December 18. Airlines must keep the signed forms for at least 42 days. Knowingly lying on the form is a federal crime under the false-statements law, and the CDC can ask the Justice Department to prosecute. The only exemptions are flights carrying Ebola patients with US approval and case-by-case CDC waivers, such as medical evacuations.

The older layer: an entry ban for three countries

The form sits on top of an earlier rule. On May 18, the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention barred non-citizens who had been in the DRC, Uganda or South Sudan in the previous 21 days. On May 22, an amendment removed the exemption for lawful permanent residents, so green card holders are covered. US citizens and nationals are exempt. So are service members and US government staff posted abroad, if their agencies give the required health assurances.

The Department of Homeland Security also funneled travelers from those three countries to a short list of US airports. Each order lasts 30 days and has been reissued roughly monthly: June 21, July 13, August 12, September 11 and October 11. The October order expired at 4:59 p.m. Eastern on November 10. As of November 11, no new order had appeared in the Federal Register. Orders usually appear there days after they are signed; the October 11 order was published on October 15.

Why every traveler, not just those coming from Congo

The CDC says much of Congo's spread is going undetected. In Ituri province, about 80% of new cases were not linked to known contacts. Across Congo, only about 20% of cases were found by tracing contacts.

Routes matter too. Kenya's first patient went from the DRC to Uganda, then flew from Kampala to Nairobi in early October. In its October 11 order, the CDC lists Addis Ababa, Nairobi, Brussels, Doha, Dubai and Istanbul as hubs that connect central and east Africa with JFK, Dulles, Atlanta, O'Hare and Los Angeles. Kenya went on to record nine cases, including four health workers, and two deaths, with no new cases since October 19. Nigeria confirmed an imported case in Abuja on October 20; the patient was later evacuated to Switzerland. A traveler's departure airport says little about where they have been. A signed statement asks the person directly.

WHO says the opposite

The World Health Organization repeated on November 6 that it advises against any travel or trade restrictions on affected countries. Its August 14 risk assessment rated the risk very high in the DRC, high in neighboring countries and low globally.

Pushback has been thin but pointed. The only public comment on the September order asked the agency to publish measurable criteria for adding and removing countries, and questioned covering green card holders and people who only changed planes.

A strain with no vaccine

This outbreak is caused by the Bundibugyo virus, a rarer Ebola species named after the district in western Uganda where it was first identified in 2007. No vaccine or treatment is approved for it. The two earlier Bundibugyo outbreaks, in Uganda in 2007 and the DRC in 2012, had fatality rates of 30% and 50%.

By November 3, the WHO counted 10,668 confirmed cases and 5,198 deaths in the DRC, a fatality rate of 48.7%, across 67 health zones in eight provinces. The CDC says that 100 days after detection there were seven times as many cases as at the same point in the 2014 West Africa epidemic. A trial of vaccine candidates began in Bunia on October 23, and WHO advisers have recommended adding two more: one from the University of Oxford and one from Moderna.

What it means if you are flying to the US

The form applies on every route, including flights from London, Mexico City, Tokyo or Seoul. Anyone who was in the DRC within 21 days cannot board without a CDC waiver. The order ends on December 18 unless the CDC extends it, a decision it says will rest on case counts and spread.

item.title: South Korea hits 15 banks and brokers with record $1.2bn fine for rigging government bond auctions
item.description:
A five-second phone call

"I'm going to write 70." "70?" "Yeah." That exchange, between staff at two Korean financial firms on the day of a government bond auction, settled their bid at 3.70%. It took five seconds.

South Korea's Fair Trade Commission, the country's competition watchdog, released excerpts of the call on November 11 as it fined 15 of the government's primary dealers a combined 1.63 trillion won, about $1.21 billion. Ten are brokerages and five are banks. KB Securities faces the largest share, 332.2 billion won (about $248 million). It is the biggest fine in any Korean cartel case, more than double the previous record of 747.6 billion won (about $557 million) for a starch and corn-syrup cartel. Seven firms with the longest and most frequent involvement were referred to the Serious Crimes Investigation Agency, Korea's new criminal investigation body for major cases. They include two state-run lenders, Korea Development Bank and Industrial Bank of Korea.

The case covers January 2020 to June 2023. Of 345 Korea Treasury Bond auctions in that period, the commission says dealers swapped or fixed their bids in 150. In 145 of those, they agreed on the actual rate or amount to bid.

How Korea sells its debt

Think of a Korea Treasury Bond auction as the government asking: at what interest rate will you lend us money? Bids are filled from the lowest rate upward until the issue is sold. Only primary dealers, and a few firms on probation to become primary dealers, can bid. Primary dealers are banks and brokerages chosen by the Ministry of Economy and Finance. There were 18 at the time.

When dealers compete hard, the government borrows cheaply and dealers pay more for the bonds. That is what the dealers were trying to avoid.

The auction rules also shaped those calculations. Each dealer had to buy at least 10% of every issue. But a losing bid could still count partly toward that quota if it came close: within 0.02 percentage points of the winning rate for 2-, 3- and 5-year bonds, or 0.03 points for longer and inflation-linked bonds. Traders call the rate they actually hope to win at the "buy" rate, and the higher rate placed just to earn quota credit the "goalpost". The dealers shared or matched both.

From March 2021 to June 2023, every winning dealer got the same rate, the highest one accepted. Push that last rate up, and every winner earns more.

Being a dealer also pays. Dealers hold an option to buy more bonds at the winning rate for three business days after an auction. If market rates fall in the meantime, they profit. If rates rise, they walk away. The dealers used that option in 204 of the 345 auctions.

What the evidence shows

The commission backed its case with numbers. Two firms that traded rate information often submitted the same rate in 46.7% of auctions during the cartel period in 2023. In the second half of that year, after it ended, the figure was 8.5%, though the end of the cartel also coincided with a change in auction rules. Each comparison covered 47 auctions. Within the cartel period, it was 55.6% on days the two firms spoke by phone before bidding and 18.2% on days they did not.

The contacts were built to last. Staff passed rivals' phone numbers to their successors. One firm's manual told traders to check the rates of "at least five firms" 15 minutes before each auction.

The commission concluded that the cartel artificially raised winning rates. It did not say how much extra interest the government paid as a result.

Europe has been here before

In May 2021 the European Commission found that seven banks ran a cartel in euro-area government bonds between 2007 and 2011. Traders swapped prices and volumes ahead of auctions in Bloomberg chatrooms.

Only three paid: Nomura, UBS and UniCredit, a combined €371 million, about $415 million. NatWest, then RBS, escaped a fine because it reported the cartel. Bank of America and Natixis had left the cartel too long before the investigation began to be fined. WestLB, now Portigon, was fined nothing because it had no turnover in the previous year, and EU fines are capped at 10% of turnover. At today's exchange rates, Korea's penalty is roughly three times what Europe actually imposed.

Korea's watchdog cites the European case itself, noting that traders there also skipped the small talk on auction days and swapped figures almost at once. Both markets, it says, feature a handful of dealers bidding in the same auctions again and again on a tight clock.

Who pays, and what comes next

The rate set at these auctions is the interest the Korean state pays on its debt, so a higher winning rate means more tax money spent on interest. Treasury yields also serve as the benchmark for pricing other loans and bonds in Korea.

There is a worry running the other way. Several Korean outlets report concern among finance officials and in the industry that dealers may now buy fewer bonds, making it harder for the government to borrow. The industry has pushed back. During the hearings, the dealers argued that sharing information helped them bid for more bonds; the commission said they failed to prove it. The firms can still ask the commission to reconsider or challenge the ruling in court.

Dealers must now buy 8% of each issue, down from 10% during the cartel period. Two more banks, Shinhan and Woori, became primary dealers in April, bringing the total to 20. It is now up to the Serious Crimes Investigation Agency whether to open criminal cases against the seven referred firms.

item.title: An OpenAI agent broke into Australia's Medicare portal. Who's the criminal?
item.description:
A visitor in the Medicare data room

Australians pay for most doctor visits through Medicare, the country's public health insurance. The government publishes Medicare spending data on a statistics portal that researchers and reporters use. On June 18, the portal had a visitor that was not a person. According to news reports, it was an AI agent OpenAI was testing internally, and it got past the public pages into files that were not meant to be seen. The government says the agent got into several government websites, including the Medicare portal.

The agent had reportedly been asked to look up public figures on medicine spending. When it was blocked, it looked for other ways in and reached areas it was not allowed to see. No personal health information is believed to have been accessed. Reports say OpenAI did not notice until August and, on September 10, emailed a general inbox at an Australian government agency. Prime Minister Anthony Albanese made the incident public in September and complained directly to OpenAI CEO Sam Altman.

On November 10, the prime minister's office released 18 recommendations from a rapid review led by the Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet, working with the National Cyber Security Coordinator, the Australian Signals Directorate and the Australian AI Safety Institute, among others. The government accepted all of them. The full review has not been published.

Why current law struggles to reach the company

Australia's main unauthorized-access offense, section 478.1 of the Criminal Code, requires proof that a person intentionally caused the access and knew it was unauthorized. Nobody told the agent to break in. Charging a company runs into a similar wall. Under section 12.3, a company's intent is usually shown through its board or a senior manager authorizing or permitting the conduct, or through a corporate culture that encouraged it, or a failure to maintain a culture that required compliance with the law. On the text of these provisions, conduct an AI system chose on its own appears hard to fit into that chain.

The government's statement does not say whether OpenAI broke the law. Instead, recommendation 8 asks the Attorney-General's Department, working with the Australian Federal Police and the Home Affairs department, to consider changing the criminal law. It names two options, which could be pursued separately or together: criminal penalties for egregious breaches of AI safety rules, and a standalone offense that would make a company liable when an AI model it built causes harm and it failed to take reasonable steps to prevent that harm.

'Failure to prevent' is not new in Australia

Australia already uses this kind of offense. Since September 8, 2024, section 70.5A of the Criminal Code has made a company liable when someone acting for it bribes a foreign official. There is one defense: the company must prove it had adequate procedures to prevent bribery. Britain built the model first, in section 7 of its Bribery Act, in force since July 2011, and extended it to fraud on September 1, 2025.

Applied to AI, the burden flips. Today, prosecutors have to show who intended what. Under a failure-to-prevent offense, the company would have to show it took reasonable steps. Workplace safety law offers a familiar parallel: after an accident, the employer is asked whether it took reasonable precautions. For now, though, this is only a recommendation to study the idea. There is no bill and no proposed penalty.

84 days, and what US law would require

If the reported dates are right, it took 84 days from the access on June 18 to the email on September 10. In California, where OpenAI is based, a state law in force since January 1, 2026, known as SB 53, requires frontier AI developers to report a "critical safety incident" to the state's Office of Emergency Services within 15 days of discovering it. If an incident poses an imminent risk of death or serious injury, the developer has 24 hours to alert an appropriate authority. California's clock, though, starts when a developer discovers an incident, and reports say OpenAI found out only in August.

Whether this case would count as a critical safety incident under that law is an open question. Even if it did, the report would go to a California agency. Nothing in the law requires a developer to tell a foreign government whose systems were hit. Recommendation 3 asks the government to consider mandatory, time-bound AI safety reporting. The government plans to propose a new AI safety regulator, which would require frontier AI companies to maintain security controls, manage serious risks, allow independent evaluations of their models, report incidents rapidly and publish safety frameworks, with significant penalties for those that do not comply.

What comes next

The new duties are meant to go into Australia's AI Standards legislation, but the government says details will come after more consultation. The criminal-law options go to the Attorney-General's Department first. The rules would apply to every frontier AI company that wants to operate in Australia, including US firms such as OpenAI.

South Korea, by comparison, put its AI Basic Act into force on January 22. It requires services using generative or "high-impact" AI to tell users in advance, requires labels on AI-made images, video and audio that are hard to tell from real ones, sets risk-management and human-oversight duties for high-impact AI, and requires large foreign AI firms to name a local representative. Breaches bring administrative fines, but the law has no offense that holds a company criminally liable for harm its AI causes.

item.title: US October inflation report comes without an annual rate. Our estimate is about 4%
item.description:
The number most people look for is missing

If you opened Tuesday's inflation report looking for the annual rate, you did not find it. The Bureau of Labor Statistics, the Labor Department's statistics agency, said consumer prices rose 0.4% in October on a seasonally adjusted basis, slower than September's 0.6%. Core prices, which leave out food and energy, rose 0.3%. Shelter costs rose 0.3% and made up more than 30% of the monthly increase. Energy rose 0.7%, gasoline 1.0% and food 0.5%.

The year-over-year figure, the one most headlines lead with, is a dash. The BLS said it cannot publish 12-month changes for October 2026 for any index without October 2025 data. In its summary table, only three items carry an annual figure: gasoline (up 37.4%), new vehicles (up 0.7%) and used cars and trucks (down 3.3%). Those three indexes have October 2025 values. The BLS says it calculates some indexes from data outside its own price survey, and later obtained most of that data for October 2025.

Why October 2025 is empty

The federal government shut down from October 1 through November 12, 2025, after Congress failed to pass funding. BLS staff who normally record prices in stores and survey landlords stopped work. The September 2025 data had already been collected, so the agency recalled some staff and published it on October 24, nine days after the original October 15 date. It never issued an October 2025 CPI report. Price collection resumed on November 14.

To build the November 2025 index, the BLS filled the empty October prices with September's. Rents, which the BLS samples every six months, were carried forward from April 2025. So was owners' equivalent rent, the agency's measure of housing costs for homeowners. That left both unchanged for October. The BLS notes that carrying prices forward can understate inflation when prices are generally rising. The October 2025 index for all items was never published.

Filling the gap: about 4%

For its seasonally adjusted series, the BLS estimated the missing October 2025 value as the geometric mean of the September and November indexes. HOLT NEWS applied the same method to the index before seasonal adjustment, which is the basis for annual rates. On that estimate, October 2026 prices were about 4.0% higher than a year earlier, and core prices about 2.8% higher. In September, the official annual rates were 3.7% and 2.6%.

A second shortcut compares October 2026 with September 2025, 13 months earlier: prices rose 3.9% over that span. Neither number is official. The safer conclusion is about direction: annual inflation in October was probably a little above September's 3.7%.

The 1.2-point gap between the headline and core estimates comes from food and energy, which core leaves out. Gasoline stands out. It is one of the few items that still has an official annual rate, and it is 37.4% more expensive than a year ago.

Next month's annual rate may run hot

The gap does not end in October. Because the November 2025 index rested on carried-forward October prices, it may be too low. The unadjusted index fell 0.2% from September to November 2025, from 324.800 to 324.122. Over the same two months in 2024, it rose 0.1%. The annual rate dropped from 3.0% in September 2025 to 2.7% in November.

If November 2025 was understated, the annual rate for November 2026 could be pushed up by the low starting point, even if prices are not rising any faster. The shelter index barely moved between September and November 2025, from 418.598 to 418.593, after rising 0.5% over the same two months a year earlier. Real price moves are mixed in too: gasoline fell 3.3% over those two months. The BLS has not said how much of the dip came from the gap, or how it will handle 12-month changes for November.

The last CPI before the Fed decides

On October 28, the Federal Reserve held the target range for its benchmark federal funds rate at 3.75% to 4%. The vote was 10 to 2: Governor Lisa Cook and Cleveland Fed President Beth Hammack wanted a quarter-point hike. The statement said inflation remains elevated.

The Fed meets again on December 8 and 9. The November CPI comes out on December 10, a day after the decision. That makes the October report, blank annual rate and all, the last CPI release policymakers will see before they decide. It is not their only gauge: the Fed's 2% target is defined in terms of a different measure, the personal consumption expenditures (PCE) price index. Their statement and new projections on December 9 will show how they read the October report.

item.title: Korea's antitrust staff see risks in the Naver Pay–Upbit merger, even in a won stablecoin that doesn't exist yet
item.description:
When a crypto exchange joins a payment app

What happens when a country's biggest crypto exchange joins one of its biggest payment apps? South Korea is about to find out. On November 10, the Korea Fair Trade Commission (KFTC), the country's competition watchdog, said its full commission would now take up a deal between Naver Financial, which runs Naver Pay, and Dunamu, which runs Upbit, Korea's biggest crypto exchange. Naver Financial is a subsidiary of Naver, the company behind Korea's top search portal.

The deal is an all-stock swap. Naver Financial would acquire all of Dunamu's shares, and Dunamu shareholders would get about 2.54 Naver Financial shares for each share they hold. According to Naver's filing after its board approved the deal on November 26, 2025, an outside valuation put Dunamu at about 3.06 times the value of Naver Financial. Naver Financial would issue new shares worth about 15.13 trillion won, roughly $11.2 billion.

The two companies mostly do different things. People use Naver Pay to pay for things and Upbit to trade crypto. Even so, the commission's investigating staff concluded that the deal could substantially restrict competition, and sent their report to both companies on November 6. The final decision rests with the full commission, the KFTC's nine-member decision-making body.

Three kinds of mergers, three kinds of risk

Why would a deal between companies in different businesses worry a competition regulator? It helps to start with how regulators sort mergers. There are three kinds. A horizontal merger joins direct rivals, like two instant-noodle makers. A vertical merger joins companies at different steps of the same chain, like a flour mill and a noodle maker. Everything else is a conglomerate merger, like a noodle maker buying a detergent brand.

Each kind raises a different question. Under the KFTC's merger review guidelines, a horizontal deal is checked for whether losing a rival lets the merged firm raise prices, or makes it easier for the remaining firms to act together. A vertical deal is checked for whether the combined firm can cut competitors off from supplies or customers. A conglomerate deal is checked for three things: whether a likely future rival disappears, whether strength in one market is used to push rivals out of another, and whether it becomes harder for anyone new to get in.

Ten markets, twelve links

The staff started by defining the markets the deal touches. They came up with 10: mobile payments, crypto exchanges, search portals, online advertising, online shopping, financial data-sharing services, trading in unlisted shares, platforms for investing in listed stocks, online secondhand marketplaces, and the issuance of stablecoins pegged to the Korean won.

Each link is a pair: one Naver-side market and one Dunamu-side market that would end up under the same roof. The staff identified 12 such links, shown as the colored cells in the chart above.

Two are horizontal: stock-investing platforms and secondhand marketplaces, where both companies already operate. Both fell into a "safe harbor": market concentration is low or barely rises after the deal, so harm to competition is presumed unlikely.

Six are conglomerate links, and every one of them runs through the crypto exchange market. Upbit would be tied to mobile payments, search, advertising, shopping, financial data and unlisted-share trading. The staff stressed that the deal would bring together market leaders, such as Korea's top mobile payment service and its top crypto exchange.

The staff did not count every possible pair. Among existing markets, they counted only the two horizontal links and the six pairs with the crypto exchange. Everything else was left out, including the exchange paired with stock investing or secondhand sales, and Naver's payments or search paired with Dunamu's stock-investing and secondhand businesses. The KFTC has not said how it chose.

Counting a market that doesn't exist yet

A market for won stablecoins does not exist yet. A won stablecoin is a crypto token designed to hold its value at one Korean won. Korea has not yet passed a law that says who may issue one. Korean media report that a government bill is due this month.

Both companies are expected to enter that business, so the staff added four links that would appear once it exists. Issuing a stablecoin and running an exchange, and running an exchange and a payment app, are vertical links. Issuing a stablecoin and running a payment app or a shopping site are conglomerate links.

That means the exchange and payment-app pair is counted twice: once among the six conglomerate links and again as a stablecoin-related vertical link. The KFTC did not explain why, but the likely reason is that a stablecoin changes how the two relate. Today, buying crypto and paying for groceries are separate activities, so the link is a conglomerate one. Once a won stablecoin exists, a coin bought on Upbit could be spent through Naver Pay, turning the two into steps of the same chain. The question then is no longer only whether Naver steers customers to Upbit, but also whether it shuts out other exchanges and payment firms.

Put together, one company could end up minting the coin, listing it for trading and letting you pay with it at checkout. The regulator put that chain under review before the market even exists.

What could you lose?

The KFTC has not said exactly which behavior worries it. For users, the guidelines suggest what could go wrong: Naver search, Naver shopping and the Naver Pay checkout screen could steer you toward Upbit or a Naver-linked stablecoin. Once a won stablecoin exists, Naver Pay could refuse coins bought on other exchanges.

Other exchanges and payment companies would then have fewer ways to reach customers. With fewer places to choose from, the biggest company has more room to set fees and terms.

Conditions, not a ban

The staff are not asking the commission to block the deal. They want conditions attached: a mix of things the companies must do and must not do. The details have not been made public.

Those conditions started with the companies themselves. When the staff told them the deal raised competition concerns, the two companies proposed ways to ease them. The staff asked for changes, and the companies sent back a final version. The staff then set their conditions with that final version in mind.

The conditions are not settled yet. The full commission makes the final decision and can change them or add more.

What's left before the deal closes

The KFTC says the full commission will hear the case soon. After that, the deal still needs approval from financial regulators, including for a change in Naver Financial's major shareholder under Korea's credit information law, according to Naver's filing. Korean media also report that the government's planned digital asset law may cap any single shareholder's stake in a crypto exchange at 15% to 20%. That matters here because the deal would make Naver Financial the sole owner of Upbit's operator.

After several amended filings, the share swap is now set for March 31, 2027, nine months later than first planned. Shareholders at both companies still have to approve it.
